2d332058a0e1bed1: US data annotation operation Scale AI faces five GDPR complaints in four EU countries over allegations that it unlawfully monitors European contractors.

Privacy campaigner noyb alleges that Scale tracks contractors who perform data annotation work on its Outlier AI platform. Like workers on Amazon's Mechanical Turk platform of yore, Outlier contractors label data, evaluate AI-generated responses, and perform other tasks to improve AI models. Scale counts companies including OpenAI, xAI, Anthropic, and Google, as well as the US government, among its customers.

Scale AI faces allegations similar to those noyb has made against other US tech firms since the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) went into effect in 2018, namely violations of said regulation.
With all that work being done digitally and remotely, Scale has extensive data collection practices to not only verify the identity of Outlier workers, but also to extensively track their activity.

“Platform work seems to be fertile ground for a whole new type of workplace surveillance,” said Thomas Le Bonniec, sociology researcher at French privacy research group DIPLab, who co-authored a report earlier this month examining Outlier's data collection practices. “This would be seen as unacceptable in any other form of employment in the European Union.”

Among the issues that raised the hackles of noyb's lawyers was identity verification conducted by Persona, a company that has faced scrutiny over an exposed test environment associated with its efforts to secure US government business. Researchers speculated that the system could be used to build a people tracker, but Persona rejected that interpretation and denied having active US government contracts. Separately, Persona's relationship with chat app Discord soured ahead of the platform's broader age verification rollout, with Discord saying the provider failed to meet its requirements for on-device facial age estimation.

According to noyb, Persona collects biometric data to verify Outlier contractors are who they say they are, as well as gathering IP addresses, device info, geolocation data, addresses, and credit data of Outlier users.

In addition to the biometric identification data, noyb accuses Scale of tracking Outlier workers by collecting system data and device activity (including activity outside of Outlier work), and transmitting that to third parties including LinkedIn, TikTok, Facebook, and other analytics services as often as every few seconds. Noyb warns that the information could be used to profile individuals and serve targeted advertising.

“Such constant and extensive tracking while working really goes against all reasonable expectations,” noyb data protection lawyer Lisa Steinfeld Leiser said of the allegations. “Why should LinkedIn or Facebook know which tasks you're working on?”

Noyb has filed complaints in France, Italy, the Netherlands, and Austria against Scale, arguing that it lacks a legal basis to install tracking software on contractors’ devices. The US company also stands accused of violating GDPR rules on data minimization, which requires that companies only collect data that’s strictly necessary for specific purposes. The complaints also assert Scale violated GDPR rights to data access after ignoring complainants’ requests to access the records of what data Scale had stored on them, as well as country-specific laws in the nations where the complaints were filed.
Noyb is asking data protection authorities in those nations to conduct a full investigation and, if necessary, fine Scale for its alleged violations.

""The report’s claims are unfounded and inaccurate," Scale told us after this article was first published. "Outlier’s practices are disclosed to contributors and require their consent. We use standard tools to verify identities, prevent fraud, protect confidential project information, and ensure accurate payment."

The complaint is likely to give further fuel to the digital sovereignty movement sweeping the EU, which has begun to realize in the past couple of years that it may not be in the best interest of the bloc to be entirely beholden to US tech companies, even if such a separation may be painfully difficult. ®
Updated at 1730 UTC to include comment from Scale.

8cf41e3f91df98ee: You wait decades for a Mac-like desktop for Linux, and then two of them come along at once. AI might be involved, but even so, it's still shiny.

ZacOS 9 and Mavernix are two very new, independent, and separate projects, but there is a common thread linking them: they are both brand new efforts to bring vintage Macintosh-like desktop environments to Linux. One is explicitly built using LLMs, and we suspect it was probably involved with the other as well.

"ZacOS" is just a couple of weeks old, and both to forestall what is becoming a very frequently asked question, and also to credit to its inventor Adam Lawson, the project's GitHub page acknowledges two of the more visible LLM coding assistances: both Claude and Copilot are there. In the Hacker News discussion, he acknowledged that he used LLM assistance to make the software, and even his online comments.

It aims to recreate the “Platinum” appearance of MacOS 8 and 9 – as we described last month, one of the few things that Apple successfully salvaged from the Copland project to build a true multitasking successor to MacOS 7.

ZacOS includes a window manager, a filer, a global menu bar, a Control Panel app, a Control Strip, desk accessories and other additional apps, and more. It can network with Macs, and integrate with the existing SheepShaver emulator to run classic Mac apps. We previously mentioned SheepShaver when looking at the remarkable MacOS9.app web-based emulator, and if you don’t remember what it looked like, that’s the easiest way to find out.

The Sourceforge downloads contain a complete pre-installed Debian Linux image. On Github, there are much smaller Debian packages if you want to try installing it yourself. It's an all-new environment, based on Wayland. (Its own icons are based on Lawson's dog, Zac.) As far as we can see, ZacOS doesn't draw on any older MacOS-like code.
That's slightly surprising, because this is not the first project of its kind that we have ever seen. Although ZacOS does look to be one of the more complete ones, there's quite a bit of prior art.

"Once upon a time, a very long time ago now, about last Friday," (as A. A. Milne put it, a century ago this month) – or at least, a few months before OpenAI launched ChatGPT – we mourned the lack of Linux desktop diversity. In that article, we linked to some projects that tried to bring a Mac-like UI to Linux.

That included Ryu Kojiro’s classic-wm, which is a Mac System 6-styled window manager, and also Morgan Aldridge’s mlvwm, which aims at the later grayscale MacOS 7 and MacOS 8 look. Although it targets the modern Unix-based macOS, we also mentioned Classic Mac Finder, which aims to recreate the older Finder on the modern OS.

A more modest but easier approach would start with one of the more versatile desktops out there. As we covered in our two-part workshop last month, that would be Xfce, which can already emulate the macOS desktop layout and with a few extra tweaks make a very usable alternative. We intentionally didn’t look at themes and skins, but they do exist, and one of the most thorough is what “Grassmunk” did with the Platinum9 theme for Xubuntu. Although Windows 95 itself is long obsolete, the Chicago95 theme makes Xfce look remarkably like the classic OS, and Chicago's developers still actively maintain it.
Fancy something a little more recent?

There is a lot of nostalgia for the Classic MacOS look and feel out there, as websites such as MacOS 9 Lives! shows. However, there’s also nostalgia for how Mac OS X used to look, as well. When we looked at how to Bring back your old Mac a year ago, we mentioned Mavericks Forever – a fan site for the last OS X version to have the “lickable” Aqua look.
Mavericks is notable because it was the first release of OS X that was available completely for free, as The Register reported in 2013. It’s not easy to find today, but you can still download it.
We mention this because you will need a copy if you want to try the second new vintage Apple OS remake. It’s called Mavernix, and for now, it’s only available for Arch Linux.
Unlike ZacOS 9, Mavernix is built on top of existing software: its windows are drawn by the Wayfire compositor, and its panels by Quickshell. So, yes, this too is entirely Wayland-based.

The main novelty in Mavernix is that it contains a tool to extract and use the images, icons, textures, wallpapers and so on from a real copy of Apple OS X, so that it can draw a Mac-like desktop using real Mac resources. To use it, you need to have a copy of OS X to hand – which is why we point out where you can get one. The license agreement prohibits running it on non-Apple hardware, but since this does not require running it at all, we don’t see any IP violations here.
Mavernix is by “Pruefsumme”, who is also a YouTuber, and on their channel, they’ve uploaded a demo video of the desktop in use. We can’t deny that it does look pretty.

How well it works, we can’t say, but the Gershwin desktop that we reported on last year is still in active development and may provide a deeper, richer Mac-like UI in time. Its development is also LLM-assisted, but the majority of the tools are human-written code, much of it from the GNUstep project – which started in 1991, making it older than Xfce, KDE, GNOME, and around the same age as the Linux kernel itself. ®

9006af7c3927ecdf: This morning, Ford revealed that buyers of the forthcoming Fathom—the company's sub-$30,000 electric pickup truck due next year—will get more than just a truck. Until now, vehicle-to-home technology—like the setup Ford developed for the now-discontinued F-150 Lightning—takes DC power from the electric vehicle and runs it through an inverter built into the wallbox to turn it into AC the house can use. But with the Fathom, that inverter is built into the truck from the start. So every Fathom will be able to act as a backup battery for your home.

It’s typical: You wait a decade for a cheap electric truck, and then two come along almost at once. And they’re two radically different products from two radically different automakers that I think will reveal a few preferences from the EV-buying public. One is the Blank Slate, from a brand new startup offering a bare-bones two-door that capitalizes on features the Internet says it wants, like no onboard modem, no touchscreens, and no infotainment system.

The other is the result of one of Detroit’s big three taking a long, hard look at Chinese EVs and asking itself, “How do we make a car that cheap?” Although the Ford Fathom will cost $5,000 more than a Slate, that money does buy an extra pair of doors, modern conveniences like an infotainment system, CarPlay, electric windows, and a vast dealership network to service the car. That may be helpful given how many recalls Ford issues each year.

a44b4d5034e532d9: Last year, Google DeepMind sent gaming stocks tumbling with the reveal of its Genie 3 world model. Since then, world models have become a major focus of AI labs around the world, but Google isn't resting on its laurels. Researchers have been hard at work on an updated model that improves on Genie 3 in almost every way. And if you pay Google enough money, you might actually get to use Genie 4 before too long.

It's easy to look at the output of Genie 4 and see a video game, which is why Genie 3 caused so much consternation in the gaming industry. DeepMind doesn't think about it that way, though. According to Google, world models are a key element in the march toward artificial general intelligence (AGI). A world model creates a virtual world, but it doesn't require pre-rendering environments or programming interactive elements. You simply tell the model what you want, and it generates the experience frame by frame in real time as you explore it.

DeepMind says this technology could create infinite training environments for physical robots or unlock new avenues of rapid prototyping for creative fields. Of course, that requires the model to accurately simulate what you want. Genie 4 has several improvements that make its simulations more useful, and that's thanks in part to Google's updated Gemini models.
b783a319f725d6cd: A MIX of volatile bond markets, sticky inflation and shifting foreign exchange dynamics is creating a risk to Asia-focused banks' profitability and strong capital positions as they prepare to announce their third-quarter earnings.
While the major Asia-focused lenders benefit from healthy deposit bases, rising long-end yields and macroeconomic pressures are exposing vulnerabilities, according to analysts.

Following a global bond rout early this month where the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield touched a multi-year high of 5.34 per cent before stabilising around 5.11 per cent, alongside a spike in Japanese yields, the lingering impact of higher borrowing costs continues to ripple through regional financial institutions.

"There is a liquidity impact, the capital impact, and there is a profit & loss impact," said Harsh Wardhan Modi, co-head of APAC financials and head of Asean research at JPMorgan, referring to the pressure from rising yields on Asia-focused banks.

Rising yields would weigh on profits and asset values, which would erode bank capital and limit their ability to raise new funds, and could lead to negative revisions of their earnings per share, a metric closely watched by investors, according to Modi.

Among major Asian and Asia-focused banks, British bank HSBC kick-started the quarterly banking earnings parade yesterday, followed by peer Standard Chartered today and Singapore's DBS Group next week.

HSBC is expected to post a 33 per cent rise in pretax profit in the July-September quarter, while Standard Chartered should show a flat quarterly profit from a year ago and DBS a 3.2 per cent decline in net profit for the same period, according to analysts' estimates.
Shares of HSBC and Standard Chartered suffered declines after the US Treasury rout earlier this month, dropping 3.8 and nine per cent, respectively.
Shares of Southeast Asia's largest lenders also fell, with DBS shedding 3.2 per cent, and OCBC seeing a near nine per cent drop during the same period.

The pressure on bond valuations and, therefore, book value of banks would potentially weigh on lenders' key capital ratios and, by extension, dividend payouts, Morningstar's equity analyst Kathy Chan said.
The full impact of that, however, can be mitigated by organic capital generation through their healthy earnings, she added.

Moody's warned that Japan's rising government bond yields are inflicting large unrealised losses on lenders with long-duration assets, already triggering credit downgrades for select regional banks, including Norinchukin and Japan Post Bank .
"We do think there's further upward pressure on the interest rates market there (in Japan)," said Alka Anbarasu, associate managing director, financial institutions group at Moody's Ratings.
Beyond broader balance-sheet headwinds, emerging market lenders in Southeast Asia are facing distinct local vulnerabilities, analysts said.

In economies like the Philippines and Indonesia, stubborn inflation and rising foreign exchange volatility are beginning to bite into asset quality and wholesale funding structures, according to Moody's analysts.
Regional banks are also bracing themselves for a slowdown in wealth momentum after robust gains driven by capital inflows from Chinese investors into Singaporean lenders, HSBC and Standard Chartered.

"China's tighter offshore tax scrutiny may slow these flows near term, potentially showing up in third-quarter results," said Sally Yim, Moody's global co-head of banks and insurance ratings, though she stressed the long-term wealth management growth story remains intact.

2d2074361838a9d1: Sometimes you’ve just got to roll with the punches. Microsoft chairman and CEO Satya Nadella was knocked down recently: his total compensation for the corporation’s fiscal 2026 is 6 percent lighter than it was in the prior year.

The leader of the software and cloud biz pocketed $90.6 million, including a $2.5 million base salary, $77.6 million in stock awards, $10.3 million non-equity incentive plan compensation and $259,203 in all other compensation (chiefly security for personal travel, charitable gifts and pension contributions).

As Reg readers are no doubt be aware, stock vests at a different rate annually and in the latest full-year Nadella was awarded a lower figure, despite breezing through all of his financial and operational targets.

Revenue for Microsoft's fiscal 2026 ended June 30 was up 18 percent to $331.8 billion and operating profit was 18 percent higher - at $155.237 billion - than SatNad's $130.96 billion target. Together, these areas accounted for 70 percent of the bossman’s remuneration goals. Operational assessment including security, strategic transformation and culture made up the rest.
The executive pay scale was outlined in the Notice of Annual Shareholder Meeting and Proxy Statement 2026.

Other highlights in that financial year included a 27 percent bounce in revenue generated by the Cloud division to $214.4 billion. Microsoft added 88 datacenters to its portfolio, and had 30 million paid Copilot seats.

"The scale of adoption reflects growing customer confidence in Microsoft's ability to deliver enterprise-ready AI capabilities integrated directly into existing workflows. Microsoft also delivered 625 Copilot updates during the year, reflecting its rapid pace of innovation and commitment to customer feedback," Microsoft claimed.

"Large-scale enterprise deployments accelerated across industries, with the number of customers deploying Copilot broadly across their organizations continuing to increase as Copilot evolved from an AI assistant into a platform for agentic work."

GitHub captured 225 million users - 50 million of these used Copilot, with one in three "pull requests involving an agent." Industry-specific AI services expanded, such as Dragon Copilot for healthcare, now used by "100,000 healthcare providers to help automate administrative and clinical workflows."

The rest of the C-suite's compensation went in the opposite direction to Nadella, and saw their packages increase, though they aren't nearly as well off as the CEO, who got the top job in 2014. CFO Amy Hood, was awarded $33.7 million, up from $29.5 million. The beancounting bigwig returned $43.8 billion to shareholders in the 12 months.

Judson Althoff, CEO of Microsoft’s Commercial Business was awarded $33.4 million, and chief marketing officer Takeshi Numoto - the person that also works on product bundles - was awarded $15.7 million. President Brad Smith was compensated to the tune of $33 million.
Like we’ve said before, it’s tough at the top. Nadella’s pay was equivalent to the average pay ($215,057) of 420 Microsoft employees.

Still, the pressure of running one of the biggest organizations on the planet must be a big load to carry, especially when Microsoft is spending hundreds of billions on AI infrastructure and looking to find massive cost savings by erasing up to a quarter of the workforce.

The annual shareholder meeting is scheduled for December 8 when investors will get a chance to have their say on exec pay. 91 percent voted in favor last year so it seems unlikely any dissenting voices will be heard at the upcoming event. ®

2b15417f37127988: THE video looks hyper-real, depicting a US Senate candidate laughing at cards that read "Death to America" and "Celebrate 9/11".
But it is part of a multimillion-dollar blitz of artificial intelligence-generated political ads ahead of the midterm elections.

Reality-bending deepfake ads — dubbed AI "slopaganda" by researchers and used by both sides of the political aisle to target rivals — are proliferating across the airwaves and social media ahead of the Nov 3 vote.

"His family values are wrong for Michigan," said one ad that portrays Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed playing a board game with two people wearing traditional kaffiyehs, the checkered Arab scarves.
The lifelike ad features cards bearing incendiary statements and depicts a fabricated family photo of the Muslim candidate with four women wearing head-to-toe veils.
"Destruction of Israel and the West isn't just a game for them," a voiceover says. "It's a mission."
Front Line Action, a political action committee aligned with Republican Senator Ted Cruz, was behind the video.
It spent over US$92,000 on advertising opposing El-Sayed, according to a filing with the Federal Election Commission.
The ad carries a disclaimer that it was "created in whole or in part with the use of artificial intelligence".
Most AI-created ads do not carry such a label, researchers say, further distorting an information landscape already plagued by election disinformation.

The Wesleyan Media Project, which tracks election ad spending, has so far identified 220 political ads nationwide — most sponsored by Republicans — that were generated at least in part using AI tools.
It estimates that the ads cost more than US$137 million. By comparison, it identified less than US$50,000 in spending on AI-generated ads in the 2024 election cycle.
Eighty-one per cent of the AI-created ads were sponsored by Republican candidates or groups, 12 per cent by Democrats, and the remainder by independent candidates or groups, it added.
"AI is making its way into the 2026 midterms in a big way this year," said Erika Franklin Fowler, co-director of the Wesleyan Media Project.
She added that only 27 per cent of the ads carried an AI disclaimer, calling the trend "problematic".
The group said its ads tally was almost certainly an undercount as it was difficult to determine definitively whether AI tools had been used in their creation.
There were no federal mandates that political ads carry an AI disclaimer, though some states have legislated to restrict the use of AI or require disclosures.
"It is deeply troubling to see these deepfake videos used to fabricate political advertising," Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff told C-SPAN last month.
"And it's a slippery slope toward the destruction of truth in political debate."
Ossoff's comment came as he demanded the removal of a fabricated ad, which carried no AI disclosure, portraying him receiving beauty treatments at a salon and covering up his "ugly record".
The Senate Leadership Fund, a political action committee that describes itself as "solely dedicated to protecting and expanding the Republican Senate majority", was behind the ad.

The proliferation of such ads in the midterms — which the London-based Institute for Strategic Dialogue called the first US election in which AI is built into every major social media platform — comes against the backdrop of declining trust in the technology.
In a recent survey by the nonprofit AAPC Foundation, 73 per cent said it was "unacceptable" for a political campaign to use AI to generate images or video in an ad.
Ninety-five per cent said it was unacceptable to "create a video of an opponent saying something they never said".
But researchers played down concerns that the ads could influence election results.

"Political slopaganda is likely more effective at mobilising voters or raising money than it is in impacting candidate selection," New York University's Center on Tech Policy said in a research report earlier this month.
"Like digital memes, there may be limits to its attentional staying power, especially as we become more and more inundated with AI slop."

a43f87e712271e91: KUCHING: The Sarawak Transport Ministry is exploring additional flight and express bus services before and after polling day for the 13th Sarawak state election to help voters return home to cast their ballots.

05cc6ebf2c0d25f4: THERE are a handful of reasons why refugees and asylum seekers from troubled nations in the region flee to Malaysia.
The most obvious ones are economic need and the willingness of Malaysians to help strangers in dire need.

Decades ago, Vietnamese boat people landed on the country's shores, but refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia are now primarily from Myanmar, desperate to escape armed conflict, political persecution and ethnic cleansing.
Over the decades, Malaysia has welcomed refugees from as far as Bosnia and, in recent years, Palestine.
It underscores the extent to which we are willing to help in terms of cash, critical supplies and diplomacy.
Regionally, Malaysia is an obvious destination: a natural buffer from immediate violence, reinforced by our hospitality, migrant networks, diaspora communities and religious and cultural affinities.

Moreover, Malaysia's prosperous economy has a constant demand for labour in construction, plantation and services, enabling migrants and their families to earn a decent livelihood not found in their own countries.
Geographically, Malaysia is a regional sweet spot: free of natural disasters and accessible by land or sea, perilous as it is.

The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) had recognised the importance of setting up a branch in Kuala Lumpur, framed as an administrative "shield" against forced return to life-threatening dangers.
The UNHCR understands Malaysia well: although a non-signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention, we have never forcibly repatriated persecuted people, only economic migrants.
But Malaysia has now called out the UNHCR for its failure to resettle refugees to third countries.
As noted by Foreign Minister Datuk Seri Mohamad Hasan, Rohingya refugees here possess UNHCR cards, but so far, only 5,000 have been resettled in three years.
Mohamad cautioned that Malaysia is forced to review UNHCR's presence in Malaysia, the first time the intent has been aired since we began accepting Vietnamese boat people in the 1970s.
Malaysia's stance is justified: the international community hasn't done more to protect refugees while it expects us to indefinitely shoulder the consequences.
While concerned that third countries have failed or have an inadequate response, Malaysia will not gamble with people fleeing persecution.
Malaysia understands UNHCR's predicament: it can only identify and refer refugees for resettlement, but receiving countries decide on their admittance.
In UNHCR's 2025 report, there were just 1,800 confirmed resettlements from 5,800 submissions, reflecting the shrinking repatriations globally.

Putrajaya must press for a clear framework that defines responsibilities, screening procedures, data-sharing and measurable progress on resettlement. At the same time, a review of UNHCR's presence must consider the practical consequences for existing refugees to ensure protection does not collapse without a workable alternative.
8b9500c72e2499ac: LONDON: The widow of Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny warned Tuesday that dictators are becoming "more cunning", as she helped launch a report revealing deepening global ties between autocrats and authoritarian-leaning parties.

Yulia Navalnaya, who heads the US-based Human Rights Foundation (HRF), urged people not to underestimate the threat that "very dangerous" dictators and their networks pose, arguing they can "only be defeated if those who fight for freedom cooperate too".

"They learn from one another, they work together," she told journalists in London at the launch of the new report, which finds European far-right parties are increasingly coordinating with authoritarian regimes beyond the continent.
"They turn to their own advantage the tools that free and democratic countries give them," she said.
"They know how to exploit the financial and legal systems of Western countries, how to get around restrictions and sanctions."
Navalnaya's husband Navalny, a staunch critic of Russian President Vladimir Putin, died in prison in 2024 while serving a 19-year sentence.
Five European countries, including Britain, France and Germany, concluded earlier this year that he was killed by a "rare toxin" from a dart frog and that the Russian state was the prime suspect.

Navalnaya, 50, has become Russia's leading exiled opposition figure, touring the world to meet foreign leaders, organising opposition rallies and publishing investigations into the alleged corruption of Putin's inner circle.
Asked about US special envoy Steve Witkoff recently telling Putin he was a humanitarian, she called the comment "nonsense" and "a pity".
The HRF collaborated with another US-based non-profit, Action for Democracy, to produce its latest "Authoritarian Collaboration Index" trends report.
It relies on data from HRF's "Tyranny Tracker", a real-time monitoring tool of ties between autocratic regimes, authoritarian-leaning governments and far-right parties.

The paper reported that such parties in Europe, such as Nigel Farage's Reform UK, Marine Le Pen's National Rally in France and Alice Weidel's Alternative for Germany (AfD), are now formalising links to "legitimise" each other.
The study said the AfD had this year "deepened its relations with Russia" beyond financial support towards more "dialogue and engagement".
The warnings come ahead of imminent elections in a host of European countries, including Spain, Germany and France, when far-right parties could make unprecedented gains.

The report found that while China and Russia remain the "primary anchors of a global axis of autocracy", media and technological cooperation has become "institutionalised" between similarly minded countries and parties, particularly across Africa and southeast Asia.
Domonkos Kovacs, project lead for the index, said that, amid "global democratic backsliding", the index aimed to "shed light" on this growing "global authoritarian solidarity".
"This is dictators helping each other crush dissent," he told reporters.

fee3cc2f8742b844: The US government's cybersecurity watchdog has confirmed attackers are exploiting both critical PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, giving federal agencies three days to patch the bugs that have wreaked havoc across the web over the past week.

CISA added CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on Monday, setting an October 29 deadline for federal civilian agencies to address the flaws. The move marks a shift from last week, when the agency warned of the danger posed by PHP2Shell but said it had not yet observed successful exploitation in the wild.

Both bugs are rated 9.2 on the CVSS scale and can be exploited without authentication to run code on vulnerable PHP servers. That's bad news given how much of the web still relies on PHP, and just how many sites could be left exposed.

Patches landed on October 21, but attackers had already beaten the maintainers to it. AWS spotted attempts to exploit the flaws as early as October 17, four days before the bugs were publicly disclosed.
CISA's confirmation comes amid growing evidence that attackers are doing more than simply knocking on the door.

On October 24, Perplexity security researcher Adel Karimi recorded 35 successful shell executions across three honeypots running PHP 8.4.26 under Apache mod_php. The attacks came from two IP addresses and used memory exhaustion and disclosure to achieve remote code execution.

The attackers then tried to contact external servers using PHP, curl, and wget, although no additional malware was successfully downloaded. Karimi's findings were consistent with exploitation of CVE-2026-109618, but he found no evidence that the second PHP2Shell flaw was involved. He also warned that the honeypots used a favorable single-worker configuration, so the results don't necessarily reflect how reliably the exploit works against production servers.

Still, attackers appear to be giving it a good go. Delft University's Threat Intelligence Lab has tracked more than 50,000 PHP2Shell exploitation requests from over 600 IP addresses across 70 countries. Of those, 171 addresses went beyond probing for vulnerable servers and started sending exploit code or malware droppers.

CISA's confirmation also comes after some of the earlier reports of successful PHP2Shell attacks turned out to be rather premature. Sophos walked back its initial assessment after determining that the activity it observed amounted to scanning and failed attempts, while Palo Alto Networks withdrew claims linking the vulnerabilities to an intrusion at a European government agency.

CISA has not disclosed which organizations have been compromised or provided details of the attacks behind its decision to add the flaws to KEV. The listing confirms that the agency considers both vulnerabilities actively exploited, but it does not confirm how many production systems have been successfully breached.
For federal agencies, the clock is now ticking. CISA is also urging organizations outside the federal government to prioritize the fixes, although the deadline does not apply to them.

Admins should update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35, depending on their release branch. Those running older, unsupported versions face the added headache of upgrading or obtaining vendor-supported fixes, while systems that cannot be secured should be taken offline until the risk is addressed.

de7ff22d19c8ab60: CAIRO: Egyptian security forces detained prominent Egyptian journalist Lina Attalah, the chief editor of leading independent news website Mada Masr, after her trial hearing on Tuesday, her outlet reported.

A court fined Attalah three million Egyptian pounds (around US$53,400) for operating the website without a licence, the maximum possible penalty for the misdemeanour she was charged with, and ordered Mada's closure.

"Security personnel then surrounded Attalah, lifted her off the ground and took her out of the courtroom, where she remains in custody in the courthouse," said the independent media, which says it has not received a response from authorities about its licence application since 2023.
Her trial marks what rights groups have described as a sharp escalation in Cairo's crackdown on press freedom.
It comes weeks after the high-profile arrest of an entire fact-checking newsroom, on charges of fake news, which are frequently levelled against media seen to be critical of the government.
Hossam Bahgat, head of prominent rights group the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), was present at the court and gave AFP an account of events.
After a brief recess during the hearing Tuesday, the defence team said the judge ordered the room cleared except for Attalah and her lawyers, before security officers also entered the room.
Attalah's eight-person defence team had made procedural requests denied by the court, which then announced it had appointed its own lawyer for the journalist.

"In a move that astonished all those present, the judge recorded in the official court minutes that the court had appointed a lawyer from the Lawyers' Syndicate to represent the defence," Bahgat said.
"Lina herself spoke up to object to this lawyer being appointed to represent her, which the judge refused to record in the court minutes."
"In an even more shocking turn, the judge proceeded to dictate motions on behalf of this lawyer -- who had not uttered a single word -- and entered them into the official record," he added.

The judge then announced the three million Egyptian pound fine and ordered Mada's closure "amid shouts and protests from the defence", before Attalah was detained by the security personnel in the room.
Her defence team is currently trying to secure her release on bail.
'Wiping out' free press'
This is the sixth case brought against Attalah and Mada Masr in as many years, but none has ever gone to trial.
Egypt, which has long faced criticism over its crackdown on press freedoms, is currently holding 26 journalists in connection with their work, according to an EIPR tally.

The current crackdown "can only mean that Egypt's security agencies are moving from years of harassing independent media to wiping them out completely," Bahgat had told AFP when Attalah was referred to trial.
Reporters Without Borders (RSF) branded the court's decision as "outrageous".
"This shameful ruling must be overturned immediately, and Lina Atallah released at once!" the group said in a statement.
Earlier this month, six journalists from fact-checking platform Matsadaash were charged with terrorism offences, after being arrested in a series of raids in September.
EIPR, which represents the journalists, said they had reported torture following their arrests, allegations denied by the interior ministry.
Authorities accused them of links to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood and spreading "rumours and false news" to undermine confidence in state institutions and incite people to protest.
They are currently being held on pretrial detention, which rights groups say can be extended for months or years before detainees are released or face trial.

5f7fa0d561693f82: From Sameer Khan
When I was growing up, almost every boy dreamed of becoming a policeman. It was a simple dream, born out of the games we played and the heroes we imagined ourselves to be.

In households, the older brother would be the first to wear the badge of authority, with a pair of toy handcuffs ready to complete the uniform. He would arrest the villain, usually one of his younger siblings, and the living room would become a police station.

But if you happened to be the only male child, only one person was worthy of the criminal role – your father. With all seriousness as a child, we will place those handcuffs around our father's wrists. He would play along, surrendering himself to the authority of a little boy who, only moments earlier, could barely tie his own shoelaces.
Looking back, it was never about catching a criminal. It was about feeling brave and heroic. For a while, we were the good guys, protecting a world that existed in our imagination.

Malaysian Border Control and Protection Agency director-general Shuhaily Zain, now facing charges involving junior police officers, deserves neither condemnation before trial nor unquestioning defence because of his rank. The law must be allowed to establish the facts.
What matters is that the process remains fair with evidence speaking louder than speculation and public confidence is protected.

In the end, an institution's strength lies not in protecting its own, but in ensuring that justice is served without fear or favour. However, there is also another court that sits every day, without a judge, without lawyers and without the need to wait for evidence to be tested.

It is the court of public opinion. Its verdicts can be swift, unforgiving and difficult to reverse. In an age when every allegation finds its way onto our screens, reputations can be damaged long before the courts have had their say.
Yet, when public confidence in an institution is already under strain, even one more controversy can reopen old wounds.
The question is no longer simply whether an individual is guilty, but whether the institution itself has done enough to earn the public's trust.
The numbers deserve our attention and so I did a little research.

Figures presented in Parliament show that criminal cases involving police personnel rose from 378 in 2023 to 407 in 2024 and 463 in 2025. Deaths in police custody increased from 12 to 13 and then 22 over the same period.
Meanwhile, rights group Suara Rakyat Malaysia documented more than 190 instances of police misconduct in 2024, with half of the cases receiving no action beyond investigation.
These figures do not establish guilt in any individual case, but they do explain why human rights groups continue to demand greater transparency.

When the public repeatedly hears questions raised about those entrusted to uphold the law, silence and pause can no longer be the response. Institutions must answer not merely with assurances, but with evidence that accountability is real.

KLIA is not merely a gateway to Malaysia. It is a strategic point in a global battle against drug trafficking. The sharp rise in drug cases and seizures reported in 2026 should concern every Malaysian.

International syndicates do not care about our reputation and our laws as well as the lives they destroy. They look for weaknesses and exploit them. This is precisely why enforcement must be firm and intelligence must be effective, with every allegation of wrongdoing investigated thoroughly and if any found guilty, they must be handled tactfully.
At stake is not simply the security of our borders, but the credibility of the institutions entrusted to protect them.
As children, there was something special about the idea of upholding the law, catching the bad guy and standing on the side of what was right.

As adults, we place that same hope in those entrusted with protecting our nation, particularly those guarding our borders. We expect them to rise above personal differences and serve a greater purpose.
Of course, the truth must be established by evidence, not assumption. But the questions deserve to be asked.
Perhaps the real question is not who wears and holds the badge and rank, or who stands accused. It is whether we have built an institution where truth can stand on its own, without fear or favour.

For in the end, a uniform may command respect, and rank may demand obedience, but neither can command the truth. And when the dust settles, we must ask ourselves one simple question: Are we teaching the next generation to uphold the law, or merely to learn how to use it against one another?
Sameer Khan is an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

8a823511a2d42568: SEATTLE: Boeing posted a bigger third-quarter loss than expected on Tuesday, as supply-chain challenges and production delays in its commercial airplane division overshadowed stronger margins across the rest of the company.

Shares of the US planemaker fell 2.5% in premarket trading even as Boeing continues to recover from years of crises and controversies that dented its reputation, drained cash and saddled it with a heavy debt load.

During the quarter, Boeing secured certification for the 737 MAX 7 from US regulators, won the US Navy's sixth-generation F/A-XX fighter contract and generated free cash flow for another quarter, while certification of the larger MAX 10 followed in October.

"Expectations are rising, and they should. We have a stronger foundation than a year ago, but we also have more work to do to deliver on our backlog, strengthen our culture, and improve how we work every day," CEO Kelly Ortberg said in a memo to employees after the results.
Boeing reported an adjusted loss of 34 cents per share for the quarter through September, compared with market expectation of 21 cents, according to data compiled by LSEG.
Revenue at Boeing Commercial Airplanes dipped slightly to US$10.7 billion, while operating loss stood at US$697 million and margin shrank by just 6.5% compared with a contraction of 48.3% a year ago.
The company attributed the performance to less profitable jetliner deliveries and higher production costs, including from its supply chain.

Boeing has struggled to increase 737 output from 42 jets a month to 47, which it hoped to hit during the summer. It has not been able to make wings fast enough, CEO Kelly Ortberg said at an industrial conference in September.

At Boeing's defense division, higher deliveries, improved operational performance and a US$252-million sale of a subsidiary contributed to nearly US$500 million in quarterly earnings with an operating margin of 6.2%, up from 1.7% a year ago.
Boeing Global Services earned US$1 billion and posted an operating margin of 18.3%.
The US planemaker ended the quarter with US$25.2 billion in net debt, down slightly from US$25.9 billion in the previous three months and US$30.4 billion a year ago.

8e8f0387002bfcb3: The iPhone Duo launched last week, offering anyone willing to spend $2,000 a chance to experience Apple's first foldable phone. For some early buyers, the morning after isn't going great. Despite the company's big talk about its "precision-engineered" hinge, some devices appear to have a hardware flaw that destroys the device's impressive internal display within hours (or minutes) of use.

The Internet is currently overflowing with images of busted iPhone Duos, all sporting almost identical damage. The OLED is marred by several bright lines originating just below the midpoint of the display. These bands of damaged pixels extend all the way to the bottom and right edges. Some units also show lines of dead pixels following the crease from the top to the area where the bright lines begin.

Anyone who has seen a damaged OLED panel will be familiar with this type of defect. When the layers of the display are damaged, the pixels no longer receive the correct voltage to illuminate them. Instead, they get the full driving voltage and are permanently on at maximum brightness. Some pixels can get no voltage, leaving them totally black. The only fix is to replace the OLED, but swapping the iPhone Duo's screen reportedly costs half as much as the device itself.

b5463b29c1314232: Three-quarters of corporate board members expect AI to deliver productivity gains and cut costs, yet only three percent of organizations have hit their targets, according to researchers at Gartner.
The figures came out of the analyst’s HR Symposium, where it also reported that 38 percent of companies are over budget on AI spending, and 85 percent still plan to spend even more next year.

"Ultimately, organizations will not generate cost savings from AI at this point," said CV Viverito, senior director analyst for Gartner's HR practice. "The greater opportunity is to use AI to do things that weren't possible before, such as shifting employee time into new capabilities, outcomes, and sources of growth."

Gartner claims that at least 75 percent of biz leaders are out of step with the broader organization on where AI creates value, which stalls transformation efforts and muddies how to position the workforce and bag those returns.

Organizations should concentrate AI on the work that matters most to the business, with HR helping execs to agree on the top bets based on strategy, Gartner advises. Companies should also spread existing AI expertise across the business rather than wait to hire scarce specialists, and give managers room to redesign the work around the technology, it adds.
Only about one in five employees' time is freed-up by AI, letting them redirect toward more innovative work, the HR Symposium heard.

“There isn’t a struggle to create capacity, that’s happening already as organizations redesign work,” claimed Viverito. “What organizations are struggling with is how to make that capacity usable and redirecting it to what is valuable.”
That starts - or so we're told - by giving employees the skills to take on higher-value, AI-enabled work, which, of course, means spending more on training.

The takeaway is that getting a return on AI projects is harder than expected, and companies are going to have to stick with it and be prepared to institute changes in the way they and their staff work before they see any tangible benefits.

A recent Forrester report concluded that AI will likely account for 20 percent of all business technology spend next year, yet more than half of CIOs are likely to miss their ROI targets for the technology

Another piece of research from KPMG earlier this year found that most UK business leaders aim to keep AI at the top of their spending priorities even if it isn’t working, with 65 percent planning to maintain investment whether they see immediate measurable returns or not.

How long that resolve lasts is an open question. Private equity giant Apollo Global Management is the latest to raise doubts, noting this week that the "Magnificent Seven" tech giants are reaping the rewards of all that AI spending, while the rest of the S&P 500 has seen no sign of AI boosting productivity growth. ®

57f9e735d3ff4182: Dating back to around 400 CE and made of dichroic glass, the Lycurgus Cup is notable for exhibiting different colors depending on the light. (It gets its name from the scene depicted on its surface, of King Lycurgus of Thrace.) Light it from the front, and the cup looks green; light it from behind, and the color changes to a deep red. University of Sheffield scientists have re-created the original recipe to produce a contemporary glass sculpture with the same optical effect.

The cup is considered one of the seven glass wonders of the world, one of just 40 glass cage cups that survived. Exactly why the unusual color effects of the Lycurgus Cup occurred was a mystery until 2007, when a team of scientists discovered the color shifts were due to the presence of nanoparticles in the glass—the result of Roman artisans adding finely ground gold and silver into the mix. Those nanoparticles change how the electrons in the cup vibrate in response to light so that the color one sees shifts with the observer’s vantage point.

As we reported in 2019, it’s a similar phenomenon to the one responsible for the shifting colors of 19th-century daguerreotypes due to the scattering properties of nanoparticles. The Romans added salt when they melted the silicon (sand) to make the glass, and those salts contained gold atoms. In the melting process, those atoms aggregate and produce nanoparticles, which in turn produce the colors. It’s how any stained glass is made. It's also similar to how the precise lattice-like structure of photonic crystals produces iridescent colors in nature, like the wings of butterflies, or opals.
c33c12ee79995678: KUALA LUMPUR: Police have reclassified the death of Noorizwan Zulkefly while in custody at the Cheras district police for voluntarily causing grievous hurt to extort a confession.

Bukit Aman Criminal Investigation Department (CID) director Datuk M. Kumar said the case was reclassified after a forensic expert confirmed that injuries found on Noorizwan's body were consistent with blunt force trauma and were not self-inflicted.
He said Bukit Aman's Prosecution and Legal Division (D5) had taken over investigations into the Oct 1 custodial death.
"The classification was made following a statement recorded from the forensic medicine consultant at Hospital Canselor Tuanku Muhriz (HCTM), who conducted the post-mortem examination.

"The forensic expert confirmed the presence of external injuries on several parts of the deceased's body, with injury patterns consistent with blunt force trauma and not self-inflicted," he said in a statement tonight.
Section 331 of the Penal Code concerns voluntarily causing grievous hurt to extort a confession or compel the restoration of property.
The offence carries a maximum jail term of 10 years and a possible fine upon conviction.
Kumar said the full post-mortem report to establish the cause of death had yet to be obtained as laboratory analysis was still pending.
He said police were awaiting further information from the hospital.
"Investigations are continuing to identify the police officers and personnel involved in handling and managing the deceased while he was detained at the Cheras district police headquarters.
"The investigation will be conducted thoroughly and professionally, without any element of a cover-up, to ensure that criminal justice is upheld in accordance with the law," he said.
Kumar stressed that police remained committed to transparency and integrity throughout the investigation.
He said the force would ensure impartial justice and would not compromise on any form of misconduct.

Noorizwan had been detained at the Cheras district police headquarters in connection with cases investigated under Section 39A(1) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952, Section 457 of the Penal Code and Section 379 of the Penal Code.
These provisions concern drug possession offences, housebreaking or trespassing to commit an offence, and theft, respectively.
On Sept 30, Noorizwan was referred to HCTM in Cheras for medical treatment.
He was pronounced dead at 1.52am on Oct 1.
Today, the family of the late Noorizwan Zulkefly, who died in police custody at the Cheras district police headquarters, urged members of parliament to raise the matter in the Dewan Rakyat.
They also urged Home Minister Datuk Seri Saifuddin Nasution Ismail to clarify the status of the investigation into the case.
In addition, the family sought explanations regarding the injuries allegedly sustained by Noorizwan and the action taken against the policemen.
Noorizwan's younger sibling, Nooranis Zulkefly, said the family demanded justice for their brother's death, which had now entered its 27th day.

013b7e3a51f49699: BEIJING: Kylian Mbappe apologised on Tuesday after the Real Madrid star was dropped by major Chinese brands for apparently joking about Mao Zedong in a video that has gone viral.
There were also signs of broader repercussions, with state-run The Paper reporting that public television was suspending broadcasts of matches from Spain's La Liga.
The offending video shows Mbappe saying that the funniest internet meme he had seen involving him was of his face photo-shopped onto that of "some guy – I think he's a Chinese dictator."
This was an apparent reference to a meme of Mbappe superimposed on an image of Mao.
The authenticity of the video could not immediately be verified by AFP Fact Check.

"My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world. I apologise to everyone my words have upset," French forward Mbappe said in a statement in French, Chinese and English.

Spain's La Liga also apologised, saying it "deeply regrets the offence that Kylian Mbappe's recent comments have caused among Chinese fans. These comments were made in a personal capacity and do not represent La Liga."
In China, jokes about Mao, the country's founding leader who died in 1976 – and whose drastic policies are also blamed by historians for mass starvation and millions of deaths – remain taboo.
Beverage giant Dongpeng, which during this year's World Cup ran adverts with AI-generated images of Mbappe consuming its sport drink, said it was terminating all cooperation with the France captain.
"Our company firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any behaviour that offends national sentiments," Dongpeng said in a statement.

Mengniu, China's largest dairy producer, and cheesemaker Milkground also said that they were cutting ties with Mbappe, who until now was hugely popular among Chinese fans with millions of social media followers.
"Dongpeng Beverage ends cooperation with Mbappe" was the top-trending topic on Chinese social media site Weibo with 430 million views.
One Weibo user said the "extremely serious wrong remarks... crossed the red line" and others urged Dongpeng to remove Mbappe's image from their bottles.
Dongqiudi, one of China's biggest online football outlets, said Mbappe's remarks were "offensive to China and the Chinese people."
Furore
In an interview with French sports newspaper L'Equipe, the 27-year-old Mbappe in September addressed a previous meme depicting him as a military dictator.
"There's a part of it that's funny... but there is another part that's a bit less funny because of the damage such people have caused throughout history," he said.
China's foreign ministry said it was aware of the reports regarding Mbappe, who on Monday finished runner-up to English forward Harry Kane in the Ballon d'Or award for the world's best player.
"Words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with unanimous rejection from all sectors of Chinese society," spokesman Guo Jiakun told a regular briefing.
State media outlet The Paper cited sources at the state broadcaster saying that CCTV has suspended all broadcasts of La Liga matches, and removed all advertisements involving Mbappe.
On the CCTV website, La Liga matches this weekend were still on its online viewing schedule.
Drawing China's ire
Global sports stars who have commented on sensitive topics such as Taiwan, Tibet and Hong Kong have previously caused controversy in China and been dumped by sponsors.
China suspended sponsorship deals with the NBA while the state broadcaster pulled NBA games off Chinese television for a year in October 2019.
This followed Houston Rockets executive Daryl Morey tweeting "Fight for freedom, stand with Hong Kong", referring to protests Beijing called separatist and seditious.
Adam Zhang, founder of the Beijing-based sports consultancy firm Key-Solution Sports Consulting, speaking before Mbappe apologised, said a rapid response was needed to quell the growing crisis.
"It's crucial to make a sincere statement. The sooner, the better," Zhang told AFP.
Fans made their feelings clear.
"I used to really enjoy watching Mbappe play on the pitch," Zhang Jingqi, 30, who works at a mall in Beijing, said.
"But ever since this news broke yesterday I have lost that admiration, sorry to say." - AFP

74dd9a7521050bc7: Two Democratic senators who have long overseen US intelligence say the Trump administration is illegally withholding a secret court’s findings from Congress until lawmakers renew a program that lets federal agents read Americans’ communications without a warrant.

Seven months ago, the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court objected to search filters that let intelligence analysts pull Americans’ messages from intercepted data without the approvals, written justifications, or records the law requires. The court approved another year of surveillance anyway. The ruling has never been made public, and Senators Ron Wyden of Oregon and Adam Schiff of California say the administration’s own deadline for releasing it passed in September.

The program, Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), lapsed in June after Congress failed to renew it, though collection continues under the court’s March approval. The administration’s own public documentation says rulings like this one are reviewed for public release “within 180 days of issuance.” That window closed September 13, even as intelligence officials press lawmakers to reauthorize the program by the end of the year.
