3a61d58890b40e27: IBM touts its Z series mainframes as the most reliable and cost-effective environments for certain workloads, but on Monday also acknowledged that the platform can drift towards hard-to-manage complexity that reduces resilience and therefore needs some help from AI.

Big Blue admitted that not all mainframe estates exist in a state of perfect bliss in a Statement of Direction for a forthcoming product called “IBM Z Atlas” that the document describes as “an AI-native solution that uses system intelligence to ground AI skills and agents in the context of key workflows like planning and validating changes or modernizing applications and infrastructure.”

“It intends to map a client's entire z/OS stack across infrastructure, middleware, and applications, and then use that system intelligence to reduce the manual effort of tasks like patch management, regulatory response, and sharing knowledge across every team, from systems programmers to application developers.”
Big Blue also hopes the tool helps mainframe techs and ops teams “better understand how components connect, interact, and depend on one another.”

“IBM Z Atlas intends to eliminate the leading cause of unplanned z/OS outages – changes that aren't proven to be safe – by mapping how a change impacts the z/OS stack, testing it, and validating it,” the Statement of Direction adds. “This design accelerates clients' modernization efforts by keeping experts in control and giving every practitioner, in operations or development, the same shared Z system visibility to reduce risk.”
IBM reckons Z Atlas will help mainframe shops do four things:
Understand systems and dependencies before making decisions or initiating changes
Assess potential impacts, risks, and operational considerations
Accelerate planning for modernization, deployment, and provisioning
Provide trusted context for AI-native experiences and automation

While IBM clearly sees AI has a role in helping its customers to manage mainframes, it appears not to be going all-in on AIOps – the emerging practice of allowing agents to either keep tech infrastructure humming, or autonomously find issues and develop proposed fixes.
“IBM intends for AI-assisted insights and recommendations to preserve appropriate human review and decision authority,” the Statement of Direction reads.

The multiple mentions of modernization caught your correspondent’s eye, because IBM’s many rivals often suggest the best way to modernize mainframes is by trashing them and moving the applications they run to another platform. In recent years, vendors have suggested using generative AI to rewrite mainframe apps in other languages, an idea that analyst firm Gartner thinks is highly overrated.

IBM clearly wants modernization to mean making mainframes easier to live with so that customers persist with the platform, a critical outcome as the company’s revenue spikes when each new generation of Z-series machines hits the market. Indeed, IBM CEO Arvind Krishna last week said the current Z17 generation of mainframes has outsold all others by $1 billion.

That kind of result well and truly puts to bed the “death of the mainframe” narrative that, like next year becoming the Year of Linux on the Desktop, is a prediction that never goes away and never comes to fruition. With Z Atlas, IBM seems to be trying to ensure rumors of the mainframe’s demise are even more exaggeratedly false. ®
0d9c9d598a849bcf: HONG KONG, Oct 27 — Tech firms rallied Tuesday following a healthy run-up on Wall Street as traders welcomed AI titan Anthropic’s IPO filing that revived optimism over the sector after stuttering in the second half of the year.

However, the main gains were concentrated in South Korea and Japan, with other Asian stock markets putting in a mixed performance as traders gear up for a slew of key earnings and central bank decisions this week.

In submitting its plans to list its shares, Anthropic, one of the world’s leading artificial intelligence companies, reported first-half revenue surged about 1,300 per cent year-on-year, but also flagged safety risks.

The sale is seen as a crucial test of whether the AI boom can deliver profits, and a disappointing reception could dent enthusiasm further, with traders already questioning the vast sums invested in the sector as well as several companies’ financial positions.
The filing lays out risks specific to an industry that has faced a string of reports in recent months of AI systems behaving in unexpected and harmful ways.

“If the use of our AI models results in harm, whether through use by malicious actors or misuse by other third parties, or if our model guardrails or safeguards fail to prevent such misuse,” the firm’s business could suffer, it said.
Still, Wall Street-listed tech firms rallied, pulling the Nasdaq and S&P 500 higher along with the Dow.
Seoul briefly jumped more than four per cent, thanks to strong gains in chipmakers SK hynix and Samsung, while Tokyo added around two per cent on the back of spikes in Kioxia, Advantest and SoftBank.

“Sentiment towards technology has improved as investors assess Anthropic’s IPO filing at the start of a week packed with corporate earnings and the Federal Reserve’s rate decision,” wrote Fiona Cincotta at Forex.com
“Anthropic revealed steep losses and impressive revenue growth in its filing… laying out ambitions to build AI systems capable of reshaping the global economy, even at a high cost.
“The listing plan remains in place, even as other firms have stepped back owing to recent market volatility.”
There were also gains in Sydney, Taipei and Manila, but Hong Kong, Shanghai, Singapore, Wellington and Jakarta all retreated.
Investors are now awaiting earnings this week from Magnificent Seven members Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon as well as SK hynix and Samsung.

The Fed is expected to keep interest rates on hold when it announces its decision on Wednesday, though CME Group’s FedWatch tool says there is a 70 per cent chance of a hike when it meets in December.

Oil prices extended Monday’s drop as senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan held talks with Iran in an attempt to stop the Middle East war from reigniting, with Tehran saying the discussions were “very good”.
Officials from the three Mecca pact countries flew to Iran as part of efforts to “de-escalate between the parties to the current crisis”, a Saudi foreign ministry statement said.

The talks followed warnings by the United States, Iran and Israel that hostilities could restart in the eight-month war, with some observers suggesting the period between next Tuesday’s US midterm elections and the new Congress taking office was particularly fraught.
Also in view are elections in Israel, where voters will deliver their verdict on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the country’s rightward drift. — AFP.

3f3a2b5c05298c1b: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia is expected to attract more interest as a data centre hub following the outbreak of the US-Iran war, according to SD Guthrie Bhd, giving the palm oil giant and the country’s biggest landowner an opportunity to capitalise on the boom.
Even before the Middle East conflict, Malaysia was drawing data centre investment from companies including Alphabet Inc’s Google, Amazon.com Inc and Microsoft Corp.
Over the weekend, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Masayoshi Son of SoftBank Group Corp chose locations in the country for US$50 billion in technology investments.
While the war wasn’t cited as a factor in Son’s investment, SD Guthrie president and group CEO Haris Arshad said Malaysia was the "most stable country" in Southeast Asia for building data centres.
The world’s biggest palm oil planter by acreage previously flagged plans to use some of its lower-yielding land for industrial development to tap the data centre boom.

The Middle East had been particularly attractive for data centre investment because of its abundant energy options, but the war has heightened risks in the region, Haris said during an interview on Friday, his first with foreign media since taking the helm in January.
"If you’re going to build data centres for US$10 billion, you’re not going to put it in a place where you might be bombed," he said.
"We are riding that wave of investment that is coming into" Malaysia, Haris added.

A large share of data centre investment flowing into Malaysia has been earmarked for Johor, which is adjacent to land-constrained Singapore. But as investment pledges roll in, Haris warned that energy constraints would need to be addressed for the region to realise its full potential.

Data centres have signed agreements with Malaysia’s power utility Tenaga Nasional Bhd for as much as 8.77 gigawatts of peak demand, according to officials – equivalent to almost a third of 2025 installed capacity.

More power generation will be needed if the industry is to expand. In Johor, the centres could consume as much as 23% of Peninsular Malaysia’s energy supply by 2031, according to BMI, a Fitch Solutions company.

SD Guthrie has over 210,000 hectares of freehold land, making the company Malaysia’s largest landowner, and has earmarked roughly 10% of its current landbank for industrial development, along with renewable energy assets.
The palm oil producer expects income from industrial development to account for a third of its revenue by the end of the decade, Haris said.
Even as it seeks to capitalise on the data centre boom, SD Guthrie’s core palm oil business faces a more uncertain supply outlook.
Haze and regulatory risks

Haris said Malaysian production is expected to remain steady at around 20 million tonnes next year despite a severe El Nino, although dry weather across Indonesia will likely disrupt crop development and delay fruit ripening. The company operates plantations in both countries.
"The concern is in Indonesia," said Haris, adding that haze stemming from wildfires is slowing harvesting at estates in Kalimantan and Sumatra and could weigh on productivity.
"Indonesia may potentially struggle with crop size next year and this could then become a supply problem for the industry."
Malaysia, the world’s second-biggest grower, is currently grappling with a supply glut but Haris sees stockpiles starting to decline by February or March, helping to support prices.
He expects benchmark palm oil futures to climb to around RM5,000 (US$1,224) a tonne by the end of the first quarter of 2027 on slowing output and firm demand. They are currently near RM4,800 a tonne.

SD Guthrie is keen to expand in Indonesia even as greater state control over the commodities sector creates some "uncertainty and angst" among producers, Haris said. The company’s operations haven’t been disrupted by the policy shifts, he added, which include plans for centralised export controls.
"I would be willing to double down on Indonesia, with the right assets to acquire and with the right partners," Haris said.
"It may not be upstream, but I’m quite interested to look downstream."
5b81a18c2494ac4c: SEOUL, Oct 27 — South Korea’s economy grew more than three times faster than expected in the third quarter, driven by booming semiconductor demand, central bank data showed Tuesday.
Gross domestic product (GDP) expanded 1.0 per cent quarter-on-quarter in July-September, according to preliminary figures from the Bank of Korea (BOK).
The figure exceeded the bank’s August forecast of 0.3 per cent growth.
The reading was boosted by a 2.3 per cent rise in exports, “led by semiconductors, machinery and electrical equipment”, the BOK said.
Investment in facilities also jumped 4.1 per cent, driven mainly by machinery used in chip-making.
From a year earlier, the economy expanded 3.4 per cent, slightly below the 3.7 per cent recorded in the previous quarter.
Real gross domestic income (GDI), a measure of purchasing power, surged 18.8 per cent year-on-year, its fastest increase in nearly 49 years, helped by rising semiconductor prices.
South Korea’s economy recorded its fastest growth in more than five years during the first quarter, expanding 1.7 per cent month-on-month thanks to soaring chip demand.
The data validates the “BOK’s upbeat assessment … that booming demand for chips is keeping exports and investment strong”, said Kwon Hyo-sung of Bloomberg Economics.
Analysts, however, warned that growth remained dependent on the semiconductor sector.

“The risk is that growth stays heavily concentrated in the semiconductor sector, leaving South Korea exposed to a slowdown in global AI spending,” said John Bromhead, a senior economist at Moody’s Analytics.
The semiconductor boom has also propelled the country’s current account surplus to record levels.

The country recorded a US$116.6 billion (RM476.3 billion) current account surplus in the second quarter, surpassing the combined surpluses of manufacturing powerhouses Germany and Japan for the first time since comparable records began in 1996.
The International Monetary Fund forecasts South Korea’s annual current account surplus will reach US$421.9 billion this year, the second-largest among 190 economies after China.
Semiconductor exports surged 218.7 per cent year-on-year to US$148 billion in the third quarter, according to government data.
Seoul’s Kospi stock index opened more than four per cent higher on Tuesday, buoyed by a Wall Street rally and revived optimism over the AI boom. — AFP
b31962c90af22c7f: SHANGHAI: The Japanese yen eased against the US dollar on Tuesday, further eroding last week's safe-haven gains, underpinned by a risk-on mood and a weaker euro ahead of key central bank meetings this week that will influence the global rates outlook.

The yen was 0.16% weaker at 157.73 per dollar, inching further away from the one-month high it touched last week ahead of the Bank of Japan policy decision later this week. The yen had lost ground on Monday too.
The BOJ is set to keep interest rates steady at 1.25% in a two-day meeting concluding on Friday, but signal its readiness to continue raising borrowing costs on mounting price pressures.

A key gauge of Japan's service-sector inflation rose 3.7% in September from a year earlier, data showed on Tuesday, a sign of increasing price pressures that will likely keep the central bank on track for further interest rate hikes.
"We expect the BOJ will conclude that the underlying rate of consumer price inflation is at a level generally consistent with the 2% price stability target," analysts at MUFG said in a note.

However, simply touching the target once is not enough, the analysts said, adding that the BOJ will now shift from a focus on the downside risks to inflation to a stance of monitoring risks in both directions.
The yen was among the best-performing major currencies last week, as AI jitters in the equity market spurred a haven rush into the currency.
Markets price slightly better-than-even odds of a December BOJ hike, so there is plenty of room for a rebound in the yen should Governor Ueda strike a hawkish note, said Ebury analysts in a note.
"We still favour another hike at the last meeting of the year, though whether the BOJ will be prepared to commit to that just yet is unclear."

Apart from the BOJ, four other major central banks will announce policy decisions this week. The BOJ's meeting follows that of the Fed, which is seen skipping a hike at its two-day meeting concluding on Wednesday.
The European Central Bank is also set to keep rates unchanged at 2.5% on Thursday. New Zealand's and Canada's central banks are expected to raise rates this week.

The dollar index held steady near a one-week high on Tuesday at 102.04 as a tech-led rebound on Wall Street revived appetite for risk, while investors await megacap earnings and the US midterm elections.
Risk appetite returned overnight after Anthropic's IPO filing and Meta's US$95 billion equity plan rekindled the artificial intelligence trade.

The dollar was also underpinned by a weaker euro, which fell to a near two-week low against the greenback as worries over France's fiscal health piled pressure on the single currency. The euro last fetched US$1.1165, down about 1.4% this month.
A selloff in French government bonds that drove the country's debt-risk premium to its highest since the 2011 sovereign debt crisis has rekindled concerns about financial stress across the euro zone.

The Brazilian real stabilised after it fell sharply against the US dollar after president Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won a historic fourth term on Sunday against senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.

Namun, dua hari kemudian notis pembatalan itu digantung oleh Mahkamah Tinggi Kuala Lumpur. Maka PN bebas menjalankan semula aktivitinya atas nama dan guna logo rasminya.
Dan hasrat ambil tindakan tatatertib ke atas Bersatu adalah aktiviti awalnya sejak menyambut keputusan Mahkamah Tinggi Kuala Lumpur.
Kata Takiyuddin, keputusan itu dibuat pada mesyuarat 'tergempar' Ahad lalu membabitkan ahli Majlis Tertinggi PN dan dipengerusikan Samsuri.
Menurut beliau, tindakan tatatertib ke atas Bersatu mesti diambil kerana parti itu 'bertindak bertentangan dengan kepentingan PN termasuk bertanding menentang PN pada PRN Negeri Sembilan'.

Tetapi mungkinkah Bersatu menentang PN pada PRN itu kerana percaya ia bukan lagi anggota PN? Berdasarkan kenyataan Hadi yang disebut tadi. Juga kerana PAS sudah putuskan hubungan politik dengan mereka?

Apa pun menurut Takiyuddin, tindakan tatatertib diambil berpandu Fasal 15 Perlembagaan PN. Mengikut Fasal itu, tindakan yang boleh dikenakan termasuk amaran, penggantungan atau pemecatan bergantung keseriusan kesalahan yang dilakukan.

PN sekarang obviously anggap Bersatu masih komponennya lantas boleh dikenakan tindakan. Berbalik persoalan yang saya kemukakan tadi, adakah ia masih komponen PN? Mengambil kira kenyataan Hadi pada Ogos lalu.
Dan berdasarkan kenyataan Hadi, bagaimana tindakan boleh diambil ke atas parti yang sudah 'terkeluar secara automatik'? (mengguna kata-kata Hadi). Sekali gus cease to be a component.

Atau mungkin PN percaya ia boleh ambil tindakan berdasarkan 'pengakuan' Azmin? Tentu Azmin menyesal sekarang kerana mendakwa partinya masih anggota PN waktu itu. Atau PN bertindak berdasar kenyataan Samsuri yang bercanggah dengan kenyataan Hadi seperti dinyatakan tadi? Meskipun mereka diam dan akur dengan pendirian si presiden PAS.
Saya tidak dapat elak bertanya – adakah tindakan PN ada kena mengena dengan ura-ura Bersatu akan bekerjasama dengan Pakatan Harapan (PH) khususnya pada PRN Melaka ?

Semasa PH mengumumkan barisan calonnya untuk PRN Melaka tempoh hari, ia meletak calon di 21 kerusi – membiarkan baki tujuh kosong. Ramai pengalisis juga pemerhati politik berpendapat tujuh kerusi itu diperuntukkan kepada Bersatu . Maka PN mahu menghalang itu daripada terjadi . Wallahuaklam.
Seperkara lagi sebelum saya menutup penulisan kali ini. JPPM sudah memfail rayuan di Mahkamah Rayuan terhadap keputusan Mahkamah Tinggi yang menggantung pelaksanaan notis pembatalan pendaftaran PN.
Panjang lagi kisah PN ini.

9cd29da16ab8f078: WASHINGTON, Oct 27 — Anthropic, one of the world’s leading artificial intelligence companies, on Monday made public its plans to sell shares on the stock market, revealing soaring sales but also potentially dire safety risks in a major test of whether the AI boom can deliver profits.
Its filing warns investors of dangers ranging from its conflict with the Trump administration to AI systems acting on their own, alongside huge spending commitments on computing power.

The listing would be the first by one of the standalone companies leading the race to build advanced AI, ahead of its main rival OpenAI, the ChatGPT-maker, which has pushed back its own market debut to next year.
It also follows the June listing of SpaceX, which owns Elon Musk’s AI venture xAI and saw its shares fall sharply after a strong debut.
A disappointing reception for Anthropic could dent investor enthusiasm for AI, a sector that has become a key driver of the US economy amid worries of a market bubble.
According to The Wall Street Journal, the company is aiming to go public the week of November 16, though the timing could change.

The offering could raise as much as US$100 billion (RM408.65 billion) in an initial public offering (IPO) that could value Anthropic at between US$1.5 trillion and US$2 trillion, the Wall Street Journal added, citing people familiar with the matter.
The 400-page prospectus devotes over 90 pages to risks specific to an industry that has faced a string of reports in recent months of AI systems behaving in unexpected and harmful ways.

It also reflects the dominant belief among researchers inside Anthropic that AI needs to be developed by a safe pair of hands, or otherwise see its extraordinary powers misused with China having the edge.
The filing cited concerns that advanced systems “could pose catastrophic or existential risks to society if not developed and deployed responsibly.”

Anthropic also warned that its “engagement with policymakers and public positions on AI regulation and safety could subject us to heightened scrutiny, political backlash, or disproportionate regulatory action.”

The company has been targeted in recent months by the administration of US President Donald Trump for refusing to lift restrictions on how the Pentagon could use its technology, and the Defense Department has since labeled it a national security risk and barred it as a supplier.

Despite these challenges, Anthropic’s business has grown very quickly. Sales reached US$11.6 billion in the April-June quarter, up from US$787 million a year earlier. That compares with US$4.6 billion in sales for all of 2025.

The company made its first operating profit in that quarter, close to US$1 billion. It still reported an overall loss of US$80 billion for the first half of the year, mostly because of accounting charges linked to its rising value rather than cash spent.
Much of the growth comes from businesses using Claude to write software and handle office work.
Nearly 12,000 organisations now spend at least $100,000 a year with Anthropic, up from fewer than 1,000 a year ago.
Slowdown risks
Anthropic warned that its growth is likely to slow, possibly sharply, and investors will be closely looking at the company’s third-quarter figures that will be released before the IPO.

To power its AI, Anthropic has committed hundreds of billions of dollars to computing capacity, including up to US$120.5 billion with SpaceX, about US$110 billion with Amazon and an estimated US$125 billion to US$150 billion with Google.
The company warned that if demand falls short of its projections, many of these payments must be made regardless of how much capacity it actually uses.
The company will have a governance structure that gives the power to the founders and not investors.

The company’s seven co-founders, led by Chief Executive Dario Amodei and his sister, company President Daniela Amodei, will keep control of just over half of shareholder votes after the listing, meaning outside investors will not be able to outvote them.
Anthropic is registered as a “public benefit corporation,” which requires it to weigh its goal of developing AI safely alongside making money for shareholders.
The co-founders have each pledged to give 80 per cent of their shares to charity, though the filing notes these pledges are not legally binding. — AFP

c9fbf27a49dffc66: Japanese ISP GMO Internet has warned customers the cloudy desktop service it offers as an ideal foreign exchange trading environment was compromised by an attacker, and that it had been slow to improve the service's security.

GMO runs a service called Onamae.com Desktop Cloud and last week admitted “a third party had installed malicious programs in the server environments of some customers.” That’s never welcome news but is an especially poor outcome because the servers host cloudy Windows desktops that GMO recommends customers use to host foreign exchange trading applications.

In later updates the company revealed that some customers reported “unauthorized operations were performed on their trading accounts” and advised that third parties had probably seen users’ passwords for trading services.
The next day, the company advised users to immediately change passwords for their trading accounts, and to do so using a device that they don’t use for trading.

The company has since admitted that its Onamae.com Desktop Cloud service’s “systems had security vulnerabilities, that its environment was accessed without authorization, and that customer information was taken outside the Company.”
“Some customers have also reported transactions in their trading accounts that they do not recognize.”

Those transactions have GMO sufficiently worried that it contacted major trading services, asked them to forcibly terminate all active sessions, monitor for unauthorized transactions, and to block trade requests coming from the Onamae.com Desktop Cloud.
Not paying, or complaining

GMO said it has “received a demand for money from a person believed to be the attacker. We have also been told that, if we refuse, the attacker will take actions such as publishing information about the Company and our customers.”
The attacker wants $50 million.
The company won’t pay because it feels “complying would not guarantee that the obtained information is deleted or that its misuse is prevented.”
Investigations into the incident continue, with GMO warning that 26,739 VDI servers may have been hit by the attack, and that users’ personal devices may be at risk.
The company is offering all users a ¥5,000 ($32) condolence payment and promised to make good on any trading losses caused by the attack.

This incident may have quite a blast radius, as GMO has warned that some trading apps may keep sessions alive even after passwords change. “Check your securities or FX company's guidance or your account page, and either disconnect all active sessions or ask the company's support desk to disconnect them,” GMO advised.
That ¥5,000 isn’t going to get anywhere near paying for the work customers will do to sort this out.
GMO CEO Masatoshi Kumagai acknowledged that in a blog post in which he described the payment as “a token of our initial sincerity towards our customers who have experienced inconvenience and worry.”

“We will dedicate the full resources of our group to providing a free alternative environment for six months, fundamentally overhauling our system infrastructure, and conducting a thorough investigation into the cause and preventing recurrence with the help of external experts,” he added.
But he also admitted that GMO knew the service’s security could be improved.
“Our in-house white-hat hackers had previously pointed out areas for improvement to the team,” he wrote. “The team took these points to heart and was working on countermeasures.”

“However, while we proceeded cautiously, considering the impact on service availability and prioritizing other issues, our response lacked sufficient depth and speed, allowing the attackers to exploit the vulnerability. I deeply regret that, despite having professionals on staff, we failed to fully translate their expertise into effective defenses as an organization.”
The CEO also said GMO can’t secure itself without government help.

“I've been involved in this world for 31 years, since the dawn of the internet industry,” he wrote. “The cyberspace that I built with my colleagues, believing it would bring smiles to people's faces, is now on the verge of being completely destroyed by malicious actors.”

“The ease with which open weight AI models can be combined and spread into countless attack tools has transformed cyberattacks, which once required advanced skills, into an era where anyone can easily carry them out,” he added, before claiming that GMO Group’s cybersecurity operation “has confirmed that the source of an unauthorized access attack targeting approximately 20 Japanese companies was the misuse of ‘ARTEX,’ an autonomous AI penetration testing tool originally intended for defense.”
Kumagai thinks public/private partnerships are needed to improve infosec across Japan.
“Yesterday, we submitted a proposal to the government to ‘apply proactive cyber defense,’” he wrote.

“We are by no means trying to shift the blame for our company's actions onto the government and beg for a bailout,” he wrote, but argued that unless Japan implements national-level defenses, more such incidents are unavoidable. ®
f6876aba3cfdc2e1: Saya pasti ramai rakyat Malaysia menitiskan air mata kegembiraan menyaksikan perkahwinan Bella Astillah dengan Syed Saddiq. Tersedu-sedu mak cik cleaner di pantri bersama kakak kerani ketika menontonnya di TikTok. Memang perkahwinan mereka menggembirakan rakyat terbanyak seolah-olah kita semua adalah keluarga kedua-dua mempelai.

Sejak diijabkabulkan pada 10 Okt lalu, pasangan yang popular dengan gelaran ‘BASS’ ini terus menjadi perhatian. Majlis resepsi di Kuala Lumpur, kenduri rakyat di Muar dan khabarnya ada satu lagi persandingan dijadualkan bakal berlangsung di Kota Kinabalu. Meriah!

Perkahwinan mereka sudah seperti cerita hikayat zaman dahulu. Kisah cinta mereka juga ibarat drama bersiri yang mempunyai beberapa musim. Daripada mula jeling-jeling ketika beraktiviti bersama, peminat meneka-neka hubungan mereka, sehinggalah kedua-duanya mengaku bercinta secara terbuka, disulami pula kes mahkamah yang penuh suspen. Itu musim pertama. Rakyat menunggu musim baharu.
Masuk musim kedua, episod persiapan perkahwinan, akad nikah dan persandingan kini menguasai rating. Rakyat gembira dan bersyukur. Amin!
Dahulu kita menonton drama cinta di televisyen dan panggung yang dilakonkan oleh para artis. Sejak ada media sosial di internet, kita boleh terus menonton artis menjalani kehidupan cintanya sendiri.

Sebagai pemerhati tingkah laku manusia, saya tertarik dengan reaksi masyarakat, khususnya kaum wanita yang begitu teruna meraikannya. Catatan kakak-kakak dan mak cik-mak cik gamat dengan curahan perasaan sehingga ada yang menangis kegembiraan, sujud syukur sambil mendoakan pasangan ini kekal bahagia. Mereka memuji Syed Saddiq dan menobatkan beliau 'lelaki idaman Malaya'.

Tidak kurang juga ada yang menyindir suami sendiri, membandingkan layanan pasangan masing-masing dengan kemesraan yang ditunjukkan oleh Ahli Parlimen Muar itu. Malah, timbul juga saranan daripada seseorang agar ibu bapa mendidik anak lelaki mereka menjadi seperti Syed Saddiq. Eceh!

Kasihan abang-abang dan pak cik-pak cik yang sedang duduk diam-diam minum kopi. Tak pasal-pasal kena banding dengan pengantin baharu yang popular, lengkap serba putih, berucap penuh romantis dan kacak lagi muda.
"Apasal dorang kahwin, aku pulak kena perli?" sungut abang-abang.

Namun, di sebalik cecehan kakak-kakak dan mak cik-mak cik ini ada persoalan psikologi yang menarik. Mengapa kebahagiaan dua susuk terkenal boleh memberikan kesan emosi begitu besar kepada masyarakat yang sebenarnya tidak mengenali pun mereka secara peribadi?
Fenomena ini dikenali sebagai parasocial relationship, iaitu hubungan emosi sehala antara seseorang dengan figura terkenal yang diikutinya melalui media.

Sejak zaman majalah hiburan, kita dihidangkan dengan gosip, percintaan dan cerai-berai selebriti. Kini media sosial membolehkan kita mengikuti kehidupan mereka dengan lebih dekat. Video mereka memasak, berkelah dan beriadah dapat kita saksikan, malah kita boleh memberikan komen secara langsung yang kadangkala dibalas dengan pantas oleh mereka. Siap sebut nama kita lagi, manalah kita tak seronok? Lama-kelamaan kita berasa seolah-olah mengenali mereka, walaupun sebenarnya percayalah, mereka langsung tidak mengenali kita.

Dalam kes Bella, masyarakat pernah mengikuti kisah sedihnya yang mendapat liputan meluas. Sebahagian peminat bersimpati dengan pengalaman pahit yang dilaluinya. Apabila Bella bertemu jodoh dengan Syed Saddiq, mereka melihatnya sebagai kisah seorang wanita yang akhirnya menemui kebahagiaan selepas melalui kekecewaan yang cukup pahit.

Inilah jalan cerita yang digemari manusia sejak dahulu. Daripada Cinderella, Snow White hinggalah Bawang Putih Bawang Merah, watak utama dizalimi kemudian bangkit kembali sehingga akhirnya menemui kebahagiaan. Bezanya, BASS ialah kisah benar, bukan watak ciptaan. Kedua mereka wujud di depan mata. Itu yang kakak-kakak seronok menonton sambil tersengih-sengih pintal bucu bantal.

Bagi sesetengah wanita, kisah Bella mungkin membawa makna lebih peribadi. Mereka melihat harapan bahawa perceraian bukanlah pengakhiran kehidupan atau jahanamnya nasib. Seorang wanita yang sudah mempunyai anak masih berhak dicintai dan menikmati kebahagiaan. Kisah Bella menjadi lambang peluang kedua yang diharapkan ramai orang.
Kemudian muncul pula Syed Saddiq, 'putera kayangan' yang menerima bukan sahaja seorang wanita, tetapi juga anak-anaknya. Ini besar nilainya di mata masyarakat, bro!

Video kemesraannya dengan anak-anak Bella mendapat perhatian ramai. Apatah lagi apabila Syed Saddiq menolak dakwaan bahawa beliau telah menyelamatkan Bella. Sebaliknya, beliau menegaskan Bella telah menyelamatkan dirinya sendiri dan membuktikan kemampuan membesarkan anak-anak dengan baik. Beliau mengiktiraf Bella sebagai seorang wanita yang kuat dan tabah.
Mahunya tak cair hati mak cik-mak cik mendengar ucapan begitu? Penyayang, menghormati pasangan, menerima anak-anak dan tidak merendahkan pencapaian wanita. Bak kata mereka, "meletup ovari dibuatnya!"

Namun, apabila ada yang mula menyarankan supaya semua anak lelaki dididik menjadi seperti Syed Saddiq, kita kenalah tenang-tenang, mak cik! Bukan apa, perbuatan baik memang boleh dijadikan teladan tetapi tidak wajarlah kita menilai keseluruhan peribadi seseorang berdasarkan beberapa rakaman video dan ucapan romantis. Saya hendak cakap sikitlah, ya?

Kita semua mempunyai jalan cerita masing-masing. Rumah tangga sebenar tidak hanya di atas pentas persandingan sepanjang masa. Tidak semua suami pandai berucap. Ada yang kekok menyatakan cinta tetapi rajin menjaga anak, membasuh pinggan, menyediakan makanan dan memastikan keperluan keluarga mencukupi.
Mungkin ucapan suami kakak ketika bersanding dahulu tergagap-gagap dan tiada siapa menangis terharu. Tetapi jika setiap pagi dia bangun awal menghantar anak ke sekolah, berbahagialah kakak.

Kasih sayang mempunyai banyak bahasa. Perut suami kakak yang maju itu pun adalah balasan cintanya kepada kakak. Tak baik kakak menulis di media sosial merendahkan, kalaupun tidak menidakkan, kehebatan suami sendiri.

Dalam psikologi, kecenderungan menilai kehidupan sendiri melalui perbandingan dengan orang lain dikenali sebagai social comparison. Kita membandingkan kehidupan seharian yang penuh kekurangan dengan detik-detik terbaik kehidupan orang terkenal yang dipilih, dirakam dan dipersembahkan dengan begitu indah. Sedangkan di sebalik kamera, semua pasangan mempunyai cabaran masing-masing. Jadi, janganlah kerana menonton drama cinta orang lain, kita memperlekehkan rumah tangga sendiri.

BASS menjadi fenomena begitu besar kerana perkahwinan ini mempertemukan dua dunia yang mempunyai pengaruh kuat terhadap masyarakat iaitu politik dan hiburan. Syed Saddiq seorang ahli politik, manakala Bella mempunyai pengikut dalam dunia seni. Apabila kedua-duanya bersatu, peminat politik dan hiburan turut bertemu dalam sebuah kisah yang sama. Jadi, bukan kakak-kakak dan mak cik-mak cik sahaja yang meleleh. Abang-abang pun apa kurangnya. Mulut berkata meluat, tetapi diam-diam scroll juga.

Kisah percintaan mereka turut berkembang menjadi acara media, siaran langsung dan kandungan digital yang mempunyai nilai komersial. Ada produk boleh ditaja, ada barangan boleh diniaga. Dalam ekonomi perhatian hari ini, semakin ramai orang mengikuti sesuatu kisah, semakin tinggi nilainya kepada industri pemasaran.

Namun, tidaklah salah untuk kita menumpang kegembiraan orang lain. Dalam dunia yang semak dengan peperangan, krisis kuasa besar, perbalahan politik dan pencemaran alam sekitar yang macam tak nampak kesudahan ini, kisah cinta yang menggembirakan mungkin memberikan sedikit kelegaan emosi. Kita diyakinkan bahawa selepas kesedihan masih ada kebahagiaan. Selepas kegagalan masih ada peluang. Itu yang kita seronok.
Kisah orang lain boleh menjadi sumber harapan dan semangat, bukannya ukuran untuk menghukum kehidupan sendiri. Kita jalani hidup kita dengan apa yang kita ada.

Musim persandingan BASS akan berlalu juga nanti. Bella dan Syed Saddiq akan menempuh kehidupan berkeluarga dengan segala likunya sama seperti kita, kakak-kakak, mak cik-mak cik dan pak cik-pak cik sekalian. Hari demi hari hingga tahun berganti tahun. Kita yang seronok mengikuti kisah mereka tentu mendoakan agar pasangan ini terus bahagia. Mudah-mudahan mereka berjaya melayari rumah tangga dengan baik.

Justeru, marilah kita kembali kepada episod kehidupan masing-masing. Hargailah pasangan yang ada di depan mata, walaupun dia tidak pandai berucap romantis dan tidak pernah menjadi perhatian satu negara. Walaupun kita dah beruban, gemuk dan semakin perlahan, kita pun bahagia juga, kan?

952c759b8ab88352: From Terence Netto
Stellar lawyer and retired Court of Appeal judge Mahadev Shankar died early yesterday in a Shah Alam hospital.
Born in 1932, Mahadev was 94 at the time of his death.
His death brought to a close a life distinguished by service to the law and public causes.
His stature as a lawyer and jurist made him a certainty for membership of two momentous royal commissions of inquiry on issues there were of great importance.
It was as if by appointing him, the government which was besieged by the toxicity of issues that swirled over it, could bolster its credibility.
The first commission, in February 1999, was on the injuries inflicted on Anwar Ibrahim when he was detained under the Internal Security Act in September 1998.
This was the infamous black eye incident where Anwar was punched by then Inspector-General of Police Rahim Noor.
The other commission, in January 2008, was on the authenticity of a video clip showing lawyer VK Lingam in a phone call in which he sought to fix the appointment of judges.
Both commissions were concessions to the intense public pressure felt by the government that could only abate from calm inquiry and findings by public figures of unassailable integrity.

Mahadev’s appointment to the commissions certified the government’s recognition of the loftiness of his public stature built over the years when he was a leading lawyer followed by appointment to the judiciary.
Mahadev, born in Kuala Lumpur and an outstanding student at Victoria Institution, was slated for a career in medicine but his father pushed him to study law at Inner Temple.

He began practice in 1956, appearing in many celebrated cases before retiring from active practice in 1983. He was appointed a judge of the High Court later that year and was elevated to the Court of Appeal in 1994.
He retired from the judiciary in 1997.
He released his memoir, “Summum Bonum: The Ultimate Good”, in 2021. The book is a narrative of his life and career at the Bar and bench.
A life of distinction at both spheres ought to have yielded a treasure trove of insights but Summum Bonum is not quite the plum pudding of a book it should have been.
How much of this was due to Mahadev’s loss of his sight is a matter of speculation.
But the fact that he managed to put it on record despite his debilitating affliction was itself an act of fortitude.

2242a4948b3156b8: From Moaz Nair
Umno has no desire to see Perikatan Nasional (PN) secure a sweeping victory in the Nov 14 Melaka election — a dominant PAS would immediately demand the chief minister’s post.
Instead, Umno’s actual strategy is to lock down its own 21 safe seats and remain the single largest bloc.
Leaving the crumbs to PAS and the wider PN alliance is just a temporary transaction to keep the peace, even if it means throwing traditional partners under the bus.
Umno’s recent political matchmaking has reached a level of high drama that puts the best Malay soap operas to shame.

The latest episode of Jodohku Bersama PAS (My Soulmate, PAS) has left the Barisan Nasional (BN) household in complete disarray, culminating in a dramatic walkout led by MCA president Wee Ka Siong on Oct 24, 2026.
For decades, Umno, MCA, and MIC operated like an old married couple — mostly ignoring each other but staying together for the sake of the assets.

But Umno’s recent, drooling infatuation with PAS has turned BN into a chaotic reality TV dating show. Umno’s eagerness to jump into bed with the Islamist party has left MCA sitting alone in the corner with a cold cup of tea, wondering why decades of loyalty were traded for a green banner.
A jilted partner
The fallout of this political midlife crisis was on full display at the Melaka state election candidate announcement.
MCA, which painstakingly won two seats (Klebang and Machap Jaya) in 2021, arrived only to find other promised seats gifted to PAS and its allies without so much as a WhatsApp text.

In response, Wee Ka Siong did the only logical thing a jilted partner could do — he led a dramatic walkout, only to later insist with a straight face that it was merely a “localised dispute” and definitely not a messy breakup.
Meanwhile, Umno is whispering sweet nothings to PAS while aggressively ignoring the rest of the PN entourage.
Their message is crystal clear: “We only want PAS. The rest of you can wait in the car.”
This leaves Gerakan, Pejuang, MIPP, and Wawasan wandering the political wilderness like stray cats, wondering if Umno will favour Gerakan or MIPP over MCA just to add more spice to the turf war.
Predictably, the MCA grassroots are furious. Factions are urging the leadership to exit BN entirely, tired of being the neglected spouse while Umno chases its green-tinted dreams.
With an emergency meeting called to decide if they will even bother showing up at the Melaka polls, MCA is threatening to withhold its election machinery.
Without MCA volunteers to put up posters, Umno might actually have to do some of its own heavy lifting in mixed seats.
Public contradiction
Worse still, BN and PAS are already demonstrating the ultimate political love language: public contradiction.

What the BN chairman joyfully advertised as a unified joint candidate announcement on Oct 24 was promptly scoffed at by the PAS deputy president, who preferred to schedule his own separate announcement instead.

It seems PAS and the wider PN entourage are less than thrilled about being “generously gifted a grand total of seven seats” — especially since five of them happen to be structural fortresses of the DAP.

This transforms their campaign trail from a walk in the park into an electoral suicide mission. Faced with this overwhelming “generosity”, PAS is employing its favourite strategic masterstroke: standing completely still, watching, and hinting that they might just dump the arrangement entirely to go solo.
Should PAS and its allies choose to walk alone, it leaves the remaining BN factions scrambling.

The long-suffering optimists left at MCA’s headquarters can only pray that if the green wave recedes into a solo run, they might by absolute, unadulterated luck be handed back a few extra crumbs to contest.
As nomination day looms, the BN leadership faces a critical question: Is it wise to sacrifice the last remnants of its multi-ethnic coalition just to hold hands with PAS?
But for now, Umno remains intoxicated by the scent of PAS’s massive voter base, seemingly unbothered by the fact that their own house is burning down.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

706e0dfe6bc8927b: Anthropic's IPO filing dropped on Monday morning, and the prospectus reads like a real estate agent desperately trying to sell a house of cards as an investment property:

The upsides are enormous. There are just a few disclosures you should be aware of. Sure, the foundation is cracked; it's in a flood plain, and you can only really afford it if you land that promotion, but there's a non-zero chance it'll work out eventually, and just look at the views.

Every S1's risk factors read a bit like a doomsday prophecy. Anthropic, like any other company that's going to trade on public markets, has to cover its butt. It doesn't change the fact that the company's success is built on a gamble that its revenues will grow fast enough to keep up with its rampant compute spend, for which its obligations now exceed half a trillion dollars over the next decade or so.
Burn, baby, burn

Going off the S1 filing's numbers, things don't look that bad for the Claudefather at first blush. Revenues in the first half of 2026 outpaced compute and infrastructure costs by nearly 2:1 and operating losses were a relatively paltry $693 million, compared with $2.14 billion in the first half of last year. The company is still burning money, but things are finally headed in the right direction.
Or, they would be if the company's compute spend were forecast to plateau over the next few years. That's very much not the case.
"Our ability to develop, train, improve, and deploy frontier models depends on our access to enormous and increasing quantities of specialized compute," the prospectus reads.

The continued development of Anthropic's models hinges on ever larger quantities of compute. Anthropic hasn't put a firm number on its compute commitments involving large cloud providers, neoclouds, and equipment providers, but the company's obligations over the next few years could be north of $800 billion, depending on how you wrangle the numbers.

According to the S-1, Anthropic entered into new or amended compute and infrastructure agreements after December 31, 2025, carrying roughly $417 billion in future minimum payment obligations. Since June 30, 2026, the company has entered into further new or amended agreements carrying approximately $245 billion in future minimum payment obligations, some of which are subject to contractual conditions.
But if you add up all the contracts listed, the total is even higher.
Microsoft: "at least $44.9B" — 2026-2033
Google: "at least $114.5B" — 2026-2033
TPUs from Google and other providers: "approximately $125B to $150B"— 2028-2031
Amazon: "at least $110B" — 2026-2036
SpaceXAI: "up to $120.5B" — 2026-2029
AMD: "to exceed" $20B — initial tranche starting in 2027
Nscale: "up to approximately $44.6B" — through 2033
Lambda: "approximately $41.3B" — through 2034
Broadcom: "approximately $161.2B" — starting in 2026

That's a total obligation between $782 billion and $807 billion, though some aren't as airtight as others. According to the S1, Anthropic's deals with Microsoft, Google, Amazon, and Broadcom are non-cancellable. In fact, the contracts with Microsoft, Google, and Amazon dictate payment regardless of usage.
Similarly, Anthropic's only way out of its contracts with Nscale and Lambda, which extend through 2033 and 2034 respectively, is if they fail to deliver on their commitments on time or breach them.

Anthropic does have some flexibility with regard to its widely reported collab with Elon Musk's SpaceXAI to lease capacity of its Colossus supercomputer in Memphis. The deal, worth roughly $120 billion through 2029, can be canceled with just 90 days' notice by either party beginning in early 2027. Meanwhile, Anthropic's agreement with AMD is expected to cost more than $20 billion for the initial tranche of compute capacity, provided it procures the full amount, but this can be satisfied by leasing capacity from the likes of Microsoft.

And while the timetable for Anthropic to meet those obligations remains unclear — several fields relevant to this remain blank at this time — it's safe to say the company's growth trajectory will need to be astronomical to keep up with its rampant spending, let alone ever turn a profit.
Compute = revenues, except if it doesn't

This spend is all predicated on the idea that more compute equals better, more desirable models that will grow the customer base and support higher-margin products, which is why the company is telling investors now that it's going to keep signing and amending compute contracts. At this rate, we wouldn't be surprised if the model dev's obligations through 2040 exceeded a trillion dollars before year's end.

Whether Anthropic will ever actually make good on those commitments is another matter entirely. "Our ability to meet the substantial and growing financial obligations of these requirements to secure compute depends on our ability to generate significant revenue growth," the filing reads.
If Anthropic's revenues can't keep up with its compute commitments, it could end up defaulting, which it notes could result in a cascade that takes the entire house of cards down with it.

Anthropic does have some backstops should it run into trouble paying its bills on its own. For example, "we have the ability to issue, if needed, up to $42.0 billion in aggregate principal amount of convertible promissory notes to Broadcom," the company's S1 notes. However, this only applies to Anthropic's commitments to Broadcom.

The company could also turn to equity or debt financing to pay its other debts. But if it can't make revenue targets, the company warns that doing so risks diluting shares and/or taking on additional debt on unfavorable terms.
My friend, my enemy, my patron

Worse, Anthropic's biggest compute providers are not only some of its biggest customers, but also its biggest competitors. We're talking major cloud providers like Google, Amazon, and Microsoft, which are far larger and actually profitable.

This poses a different problem for Anthropic. Cloud providers are convenient because Anthropic doesn't have to pay for the compute up front. But if the company can't get adequate compute from Google, Amazon, or Microsoft because they're using it for training or running their own or someone else's models, they may need to look at alternative options, including building out their own infrastructure.

"We may in the future finance a greater portion of our compute on an up-front basis, including through capital leases, prepayments, debt-financed purchases of equipment, or similar arrangements," the company explained.

In fact, to some degree Anthropic is already doing this through its lease deal with Broadcom. This appears to be tied to Google and Broadcom's collaboration with Anthropic to provide TPU-based compute earlier this year. Meta was also reportedly in talks to deploy Google TPUs in its own datacenters so the arrangement wouldn't be that unusual.
And then of course there are external threats, like conflict in the South China Sea severing supply chains for the vast majority of AI accelerators.
The only way to justify this kind of spend and risk is if you believe the upside is enormous. Like, the biggest economic transformation in the history of humankind.

As Anthropic puts it: "We believe this abundance of AI will rapidly transform every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet." ®

As to whether these price trends suggest that AI companies have a sustainable business, investors may soon be able to make that bet on the Nasdaq exchange after Anthropic floats. ®
2233208a03935788: Malaysia’s opposition crisis exposes an uncomfortable truth: political parties can survive organisational breakdown while voters inherit the uncertainty. Perikatan Nasional’s deregistration, although the High Court has since granted a stay, should therefore prompt a question beyond whether regulators acted correctly.
Can a coalition ask Malaysians to trust its governing competence when its own partners cannot agree on the rules governing their relationship?

On Oct 20, the Registrar of Societies cancelled PN’s registration under the Societies Act 1966. The regulator said the coalition’s response to an earlier notice failed to answer the grounds raised. Public reporting connects the dispute to Bersatu’s complaint about exclusion from a July meeting and disagreement over its standing within PN. These are reported grounds and competing claims, not a judicial finding that every allegation is established.

The High Court had already granted permission for PN to pursue judicial review of regulatory action, without suspending the restriction on its activities. PN has announced further legal challenges. Courts must determine the legality of contested decisions; political opponents should not present administrative action as proof of electoral unfitness.

Yet the underlying governance problem deserves scrutiny independently of the litigation. Coalition politics depends on agreements among organisations with different ambitions and electoral incentives. Those agreements require reliable procedures for convening meetings, determining representation and resolving disagreements. When partners dispute whether one of them belongs at the table, the coalition’s promise of collective leadership becomes difficult to evaluate.

This matters because PN is not merely an electoral label. It has sought to present itself as an alternative national administration. That claim invites questions about how it would negotiate Cabinet decisions, allocate responsibilities and handle policy disagreements if entrusted with government. Internal conflict does not automatically establish administrative incompetence, but refusing to explain the conflict leaves voters unable to assess institutional readiness.

The Melaka election brings the issue into sharper focus. With polling scheduled for Nov 14, candidates and party organisations face choices about campaign identity. PN representatives have discussed using a component party’s banner if necessary. Such arrangements may be lawful, subject to electoral requirements, but a familiar symbol cannot resolve disagreements about who authorises commitments or speaks for the wider alliance.

The same standard should apply to every coalition. Barisan Nasional and Pakatan Harapan also combine parties with competing histories and priorities. Their success should be judged not by an absence of disagreement but by whether disputes are settled through understood rules and whether decisions remain accountable to members. A healthy democracy needs effective opposition as much as a stable government.

There is a political economy dimension. Investors, employers and households watch whether leaders can sustain commitments beyond press conferences. Coalition uncertainty can complicate expectations about economic policy, even before any election changes government. That does not mean PN’s deregistration has measurably damaged investment or market confidence; no such causal conclusion follows from the available evidence. The concern is institutional predictability, not an invented financial shock.

The immediate remedy is political candour. PN’s component leaders should explain their working arrangements, who has authority to negotiate electoral cooperation and how disagreements will be decided. They need not reveal confidential strategy or prejudice court proceedings. But voters deserve enough information to distinguish a functioning partnership from an improvised electoral understanding.

Equally, the government must resist treating its opponent’s organisational difficulty as a substitute for answering policy criticism. Regulators must apply the law impartially, while ministers should avoid rhetoric that blurs administrative enforcement with political competition. Otherwise, a dispute originating inside one coalition could deepen suspicion about institutions across politics.

For Melaka voters, practical concerns remain decisive – local services, jobs, living costs, candidate integrity and the quality of proposed administration. Coalition confusion may influence judgments about credibility, but its electoral weight cannot be assumed without evidence. Analysts should resist converting one dramatic event into a forecast of voting behaviour.

The larger lesson is that opposition credibility is a public good. Malaysia benefits when challengers are organised enough to scrutinise government and credible enough to offer alternatives. PN’s future will ultimately depend on more than registration status.

Its leaders must show that collective authority can be exercised transparently, disagreements managed responsibly and commitments honoured. A coalition unable to explain how it governs itself will struggle to persuade voters that it can govern everyone else.
Azam Mohd is an FMT reader.

a039f26ea6138941: A new Miasma-family npm worm, originally believed to be just a test with no victims, secretly armed 42 real GitHub repositories from 11 owners, hijacking accounts as early as July and using a stealthy payload built to stay hidden from GitHub and automated scanners, according to JFrog researchers.

Threat hunters at SafeDep, an open source supply chain security firm, first spotted the “testmetest” npm campaign last week, identifying 18 packages linked to the same operator between October 19 and October 25, including releases containing credential-stealing malware. As with earlier npm worms, the malware is self-replicating, steals credentials, and installs a wiper that deletes the home directory when the victim revokes the stolen GitHub token, the security researchers noted.
The new npm worm shares code with June’s Miasma Phantom Gyp worm, and adds Mini Shai-Hulud’s token-revocation wiper.
As of October 22, however, SafeDep had found no compromised third-party packages or victims. “All observed activity belongs to the operator’s own test accounts,” the team wrote.
As with most happy-ending security stories, that proved too good to be true.

In a Monday report, supply chain security company JFrog said its analysis proved otherwise, and found the testmetest campaign operator “had already armed real repositories belonging to established developers and organizations.”

This isn’t just about timing, either, according to JFrog researchers Guy Korolevski and Yair Benamou. “The payload blobs were large enough to evade the GitHub search and API paths normally used to find this kind of compromise,” they wrote.

The attackers planted execution hooks for AI coding assistants and development tools, including Claude, Gemini, Cursor, and VS Code, alongside polymorphic wrappers measuring 12.9 to 13.7 MB that decode a hidden CI-publisher payload. Separately, the npm worm steals credentials, modifies repositories and CI configurations, and spreads through npm packages.

The malware also uses a compiled native add-on to decrypt and launch a separate payload. Before executing, the loader checks for CI runners, containers, sandboxes, debuggers, and other signs of automated analysis, exiting silently when it detects them to reduce the likelihood of detection by security scanners.

The researchers also found a second build that skips the encrypted file. “It forks, detaches and runs a hard-coded command that pulls a loader from a repository on the operator's own GitHub account,” they wrote. That account – CementBeetleSteeple – hosted 17 campaign repositories in total.

JFrog connected this account to a shellpanel scanner, previously documented by Socket in a large-scale campaign that abused GitHub Actions in compromised repositories to exploit CVE-2026-41940 and steal server credentials.
CVE-2026-41940 is an authentication bypass affecting cPanel and WHM. CISA added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog in April, and cPanel has since published patched versions.

“C2 infrastructure were previously reported by Socket; our findings connect them to the testmetest GitHub victim cluster through artifacts and workflows on the same hijacked owners,” the JFrog researchers wrote. They added that while they found 42 armed GitHub repositories and attempted internet-wide exploitation, they did not confirm any downstream cPanel compromises.®

ff235960aebe93e3: After two months of discomfort, a man in South Korea went to an eye clinic where doctors pulled 11 living, wriggling worms from his eyes. They apparently made the most of their time on the man's peepers; at the time of extraction, many of the female worms were pregnant. The man narrowly avoided having them spew their loads of living larvae directly into his eyes.

The man in this case was a 71-year-old crop farmer. He told doctors that for the previous two months he had the sensation of having something stuck in both his eyes, which were also red and blurry. When ophthalmologists took a look, they quickly saw the problem: multiple mobile, whitish roundworms. His eyes were not in good shape either, as one might expect. The blood vessels in the membrane over the eye, the conjunctiva, were enlarged, making his eyes look red. And the cells of his cornea—the transparent, dome-shaped outer layer of the eye—had eroded, potentially after the helminths' hanky-panky.

According to a case report published in the New England Journal of Medicine, the doctors gave the man a topical treatment to numb his eyes and then began plucking out the worms one by one with fine forceps. They collected 11 adult worms, which ranged in size from 11 to 22 mm.

e690224c4db60bf8: Sir Arthur Conan Doyle created one of the most beloved fictional detectives of all time in Sherlock Holmes, spawning countless novels, films, TV series, and so forth featuring the sleuth. Far fewer people know about the real-life inspiration for Holmes: a renowned surgeon at Scotland's University of Edinburgh named Joseph Bell, who taught Doyle when the author was still a young medical student. Bell is the subject of a new, eminently readable biography, Sleuth-Hound: The Case of the Real Sherlock Holmes, by medical historian Lindsey Fitzharris.

A noted science communicator with a fondness for the medically macabre, Fitzharris published a biography of Scottish surgical pioneer Joseph Lister, The Butchering Art, in 2017—a great, if occasionally grisly, read. She followed up with 2022’s The Facemaker: A Visionary Surgeon’s Battle to Mend the Disfigured Soldiers of World War I, about a WWI surgeon named Harold Gillies who rebuilt the faces of injured soldiers.

In 2020, Fitzharris hosted a documentary for the Smithsonian Channel, The Curious Life and Death Of…, exploring famous deaths, ranging from drug lord Pablo Escobar to magician Harry Houdini. Fitzharris performed virtual autopsies, experimented with blood samples, interviewed witnesses, and conducted real-time demonstrations in hopes of gleaning fresh insights. And last year she and her husband, caricaturist Adrian Teal, collaborated on an illustrated children's book, Dead Ends! Flukes, Flops, and Failures that Sparked Medical Marvels.

7bc0c9ce643c1908: The 2026 elections in Brazil played out amid an widespread assumption repeated around the world: that the country was polarized and that would inform the vote. But the word “polarization” implies symmetry – and symmetry is something that never existed in the contest between President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro. On one side, a moderate center-left politician with a center-right running mate, Geraldo Alckmin. On the other, a representative of the radical right and a member of an international movement that critics say threatens democracies around the world. Flávio is no mere conservative. While he may be courted and supported by the members of the Republican Party in the U.S., his policies put him more in the mold of Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany and Portugal’s Enough, a party that advocates the repatriation of immigrants and a ban on Muslim places of worship. On the day he launched his candidacy, at an event of Brazil’s Liberal Party (PL) in São Paulo, Flávio laid out three of the guiding principles of what his administration would look like. First was the so called “Project Darkness”, a crime-fighting plan inspired by by El Salvador’s hard-right President Nayib Bukele. Second was joining the Shield of the Americas, U.S. President Donald Trump’s military and political initiative for the continent. Thirdly, Flávio laid out plans for the “tesouraço” or “big cut” – a slashing of public spending modeled after Argentinian President Javier Milei’s “chainsaw” economic policy. Since he didn’t provide any details, it’s unclear whether it would be just as sharp as Milei’s, but it was enough to strike fear into those who depend on social programs to survive. Milei himself was at the launch event. He arrived singing the song The Panic Show by the Argentine hard rock band La Renga. Flávio accompanied Milei in the song’s refrain: “Yo soy el león, soy el rey y te destrozaré” (“I am the lion, I am the king, and I will tear you apart”) while dancing along with the Argentine president. It is, I believe, the form, more than the content, that defines the members of the far-right brotherhood that threatens democracies around the world. They are politicians who do not like to negotiate, even though negotiation is the essence of politics. They want to annihilate the “enemy”, as if they were, literally, on a battlefield. Misplaced ideas Flávio’s ideas are clearly “misplaced ideas,” to borrow the term coined by Brazilian literary critic, essayist, and professor Roberto Schwarz. It is impossible to implement Nayib Bukele’s crime-fighting plan — which allows for the arrest of any citizen without a formal charge, the right for legal counsel, or habeas corpus — in a democratic country. On the economy side, in the midst of a debt crisis, Brazil does needs a fiscal adjustment. However, the country’s economic situation bears no resemblance to that of Argentina, a country that has seen its currency collapse and is rolling over dollar denominated debt. A recent report in the Financial Times portrayed what is known in Brazil as Bolsonarism as a clan similar to the Roy family from the American television series “Succession.” Nothing could be more apt. Flávio is not Flávio. He is merely a generic offshoot of the Bolsonaro brand. During the Brazilian TV Globo election debate held right before the runoff of last Sunday, Oct. 25, he referred to his now jailed father administration as “our government.” If he were elected president, Flávio would have governed under Jair’s supervision and alongside his brother Eduardo Bolsonaro - a former congressman now living in the U.S. to escape a arrest warrant - who serves as the point of contact between Bolsonarism and the radical and far right around the world. Eduardo is close to former Hungary prime minister Viktor Orbán, Spain’s Santiago Abascal, president of Spanish far-right party Vox, El Salvador’s Bukele, France’s far-right leader Marine Le Pen, and the most radical wing of the U.S. Republican Party. 35ef08cfc995907f: Now, Russian disinformation fuels the memory of violent historic conflicts, and Polish empathy is burning out
Originally published on Global Voices

Folkowisko during the “Borderland Memory” project, bringing Ukrainian and Polish youth together to preserve shared historical heritage, restore historic cemeteries, and strengthen cross-cultural friendship. Photo: Folkowisko. Used with permission.

Marcin Piotrowski remembers the beginning of his work in Ukraine through the Budomierz-Hruszów border crossing in February 2022, days after the launch of Russia’s war on Ukraine. “We crossed the border on the second day after the full-scale invasion,” he says, “and there were hundreds of people there. Nobody was helping them.”

People were waiting for days to enter Poland, some in cars and some on foot, as temperatures fell to around minus 15 degrees Celsius. On the Polish side, food and transport had been organised, but the queues on the Ukrainian side had become a challenge of their own. Piotrowski and volunteers from his Polish association, Folkowisko, decided to intervene. “We had experience because our association organises festivals,” he explains. “We put up tents, brought volunteers, and our medical service from the festival came as well. Later, we started helping at other border crossings, then in Lviv at the railway station, and we began working with volunteers from different parts of Ukraine.”

What began as emergency assistance developed into a network of projects across the Polish-Ukrainian border. Folkowisko helped establish a medical clinic and education centre in Nakhachiv, near the Polish border, where Polish and Ukrainian cultural workers have held joint workshops. The organisation has also supported psychological care, trained Ukrainian psychologists and social workers, and brought Ukrainian families affected by the war to Poland for temporary respite.

But Folkowisko's work is not only about the present. Piotrowski is also interested in the history of the border region, and in what happens when difficult memories are discussed through contact rather than isolation. “Before the Second World War, there were more than a thousand Ukrainians in the village where we work,” he says, referring to a locality in what is now eastern Poland. “Today, there are 43 people and they are all Polish. People were resettled in 1945 and 1947, during Operation Vistula. This was a place where Jews, Poles and Ukrainians lived together, and 80 years ago you could not really say where the border was.”

The history separating the two societies is particularly painful. During World War II, tens of thousands of Polish civilians were killed by Ukrainian nationalist formations in the Volhynia region. Polish nationalist groups retaliated, killing thousands of Ukrainian civilians. The competing memories of these events have remained politically sensitive, especially in families whose relatives were victims.

After the fall of communism, the history of Volhynia became increasingly prominent in Polish public debate. In Ukraine, meanwhile, the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) acquired an important place in national memory because of its role in the struggle for Ukrainian independence against Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union. Disputes over monuments, commemorations, exhumations and historical figures have repeatedly affected relations between Warsaw and Kyiv.

The subject is also vulnerable to manipulation, according to Łukasz Wojtkowski, an assistant professor at Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń, who researches information operations and disinformation. He argues that historical grievances can be connected to contemporary fears and used to deepen divisions: “Volhynia is a playbook for propaganda and disguised disinformation,” he explains. “It is basically the only open case between those two nations that can spark the engine of disinformation and hatred. Russia can put two irons in the fire at the same time: it can increase the hatred between Poland and Ukraine, and it can reinforce the Russian narrative that there is a fascist regime in Kyiv.”

Anna Mierzyńska, a Polish journalist and social media researcher specialising in disinformation, has studied similar narratives targeting Polish audiences. “Reliable historical debate,” she stresses, “is always based on listening to both sides and taking new developments into account. Its purpose is not to attack or create hatred, but to explain what happened and find an understanding.” While there is such a debate among historians and experts, she adds that in the Polish information sphere, “many of the posts on this subject are designed to provoke hatred toward Ukrainians.”

Recurring narratives portray Ukrainians as a physical threat to Poles, Mierzyńska continues, using descriptions of the Volhynia crimes to create fear, or to suggest that Ukrainians could seek Polish territory. Existing social problems can also be folded into the same narrative. Long waiting lists for healthcare, for example, existed before the arrival of millions of Ukrainian refugees, but online claims blamed Ukrainians for them. Housing, employment and public services have been framed in similar ways.

The scale of Ukrainian displacement makes the relationship especially important. In 2026, nearly a million Ukrainians took temporary protection in Poland, representing 21.8 percent of all people from Ukraine under temporary protection in the European Union.

We need good contacts between Poles and Ukrainians, integration, getting to know each other and building trust. When we know each other well and trust each other, outside influence becomes much less important. – Anna Mierzyńska

For Piotrowski, the first months after the invasion demonstrated what such contact can look like. “Ordinary citizens living on the border with Ukraine were the first ones to provide immediate support,” he recalls. “I have never seen so much kindness in my life on both sides of the border, and so much reconciliation and understanding.”

Five years into the full-scale war, however, the border has also revealed the limits of that extraordinary solidarity. “I understand that when Poles opened their homes, it could become difficult,” Piotrowski says. “Someone comes who speaks another language, has slightly different customs and wants to stay for a long time. This is what I call empathy burnout.”

He does not regard that exhaustion as proof that the solidarity of 2022 was false, but rather, as a relationship being tested by time. His response is the same one that drives Folkowisko’s cultural work: more contact. “Poles don't know Ukrainians, Ukrainians don't know Poles,” he says. “Our job is to make people meet each other and understand each other.”

This approach means bringing difficult history into conversations in much the same way that Folkowisko’s festivals and programmes bring Polish and Ukrainian participants together while addressing the violence and displacement that transformed the region.

Wojtkowski is more cautious about whether historical reconciliation alone could resolve the wider conflict over competing narratives. “Imagine that tomorrow Poland and Ukraine commemorate every victim, Ukraine admits who was killed and how many people died, Poland admits what happened on its side, and all the exhumations are completed,” he posits. “It would not change everything, because Russia has other narratives.”

He maintains that, when it comes to history, both Polish and Ukrainian society did not do their homework properly. “In Poland, we learned the story of the interwar period as the restoration of the Polish state after more than a hundred years without independence,” he says, “but we did not always learn enough about the Ukrainian experience within that state. Ukraine has its own work to do in confronting everything that happened during the Second World War.”

Wojtkowski further advises that both Poland and Ukraine “should step very carefully, as if on very thin ice.” According to him, there should be signs of goodwill and a willingness to cooperate, but there is still a lot to do politically, academically and socially.

For Piotrowski, however, governments and historians do not have to resolve everything before ordinary people can build relationships: “We are trying to connect people who live ten or 15 kilometres from each other. They have different memories, different histories, but they can still meet and work together.”

As Ukraine moves toward the European Union, and as Polish and Ukrainian lives become increasingly intertwined, those everyday relationships may shape how the two societies handle their shared past. “If we lose the contact between ordinary people across both countries,” Piotrowski maintains, “then it becomes much easier to build the walls. And once the walls are there, it is much harder to build the bridges again.”
