4b22ee1f7844c295: Being Mozambican is a matter of belonging — regardless of one’s origin, appearance, or surname
Originally published on Global Voices
Indians in Mozambique celebrating the Hindu festival of Navratri. Image by Kash_if via Flickr. CC BY 2.0.

In Mozambique, the word monhé has a much deeper history than its everyday use might suggest. Depending on who says it and the context, it can simply be a reference to the population of Indian origin, an identity marker, or a prejudiced remark. But behind the word there is a history of migration, trade, colonialism, independence, displacement, and, above all, belonging.

The question of who is Mozambican gets particularly interesting when we look at the communities of Indian origin, who have lived in the country for several generations. Are they Mozambicans? Indians? Foreigners? Or, in some cases, stateless persons? The answer cannot be found in appearance, surname, religion, or family origin alone. It is found in the country’s history and, particularly, in its nationality law.
A presence older than modern borders

The presence of people originating from the Indian subcontinent in the lands we now call Mozambique predates the country’s independence and, in many instances, predates the demarcation of the current political borders. The Indian Ocean’s trade networks connected the East African coast to South Asia long before 1975, the year Mozambique gained its independence. Over time, merchants, families, and whole communities settled in different parts of the country.

During the Portuguese colonial period, this took place within a political structure that gave people nationalities and legal statuses according to the rules of the empire. As such, “being of Indian origin” never meant automatically “being an Indian citizen.” A person can have Indian ancestry and at the same time hold Portuguese, Indian, Pakistani, or any other nationality, which could leave people in a complex bureaucratic situation. This distinction became especially important when the empire came to an end.
1975: When the question “Whose country is this?” took on a new meaning

Mozambique’s independence, made official on June 25th, 1975, did not just mean a transfer of political power. It also implied the need to define who would legally receive the new state, which was known as the New State. The Nationality Law of 1975 was key to answering that question. Among its provisions were rules that recognized as Mozambicans certain people born in the territory and resident in Mozambique at the time of independence, as well as other criteria related to birth, family links, and residence. The legislation would thus transform a heterogeneous imperial population into a national political community.

For many families of Indian origin who lived in Mozambique for decades or generations, this transformation would mean a fundamental change: no longer being legally associated with a colonial power or a foreign nationality and becoming part of the new Mozambican nation. But the experience of this transition was not the same for everybody.
When identity doesn’t fit neatly into a passport

Decolonization created situations where identity, origin, and nationality did not match. Imagine a family history across three generations: the grandparents born in India, the parents born in Mozambique during the colonial period, and the children born after independence. Which nationality should each generation have? The answer may depend on specific legal circumstances: place of birth, the parents’ nationality, residence in Mozambique at its independence, existing documentation, and any decisions to opt for or relinquish nationality.

Here, the issue of statelessness arises. A stateless person is somebody who is not considered a national by any state’s legislation. It is not an ambiguous cultural identity or feeling divided between two countries, but a legal status.

After decolonization, some people in former colonial territories, such as Angola and Mozambique, faced this problem: some were no longer recognized as nationals by the former colonial power without any other nationalities automatically being granted. This does not mean, though, that the whole Indian community in Mozambique became stateless. This generalization would be historically and legally incorrect.
“Monhé” is not a nationality

This may be where everyday language misleads us. The term “Monhé” may be used as an identity category, but it is not a legal category. Somebody called a monhé can be as Mozambican as anybody else born or naturalized in the country. They may have been born in Maputo, Nampula, Beira, or Quelimane, speak Portuguese or another Mozambican language, have had family in Mozambique for several generations, and never have lived in India. Your ancestry does not disqualify your citizenship.

Likewise, a person of Indian origin living in Mozambique can be a citizen of another country. And, in certain cases, they may have difficulties in proving or acquiring a nationality. As such, it is important to distinguish three concepts that are often confused: origin, nationality, and citizenship. A person’s origin may be Indian. Their identity can be simultaneously Mozambican and Indian. Nationality, though, is a legal relationship between an individual and a state.
A community across oceans
The history of so-called monhés in Mozambican identity also challenges an overly simplistic view of nationality.

Mozambique has always been a space where people cross paths. Africans, Arabs, Indians, Portuguese, and other peoples participated, at different moments, in the country’s social, economic, and cultural development. The Mozambican coast, in particular, cannot be understood without movements across the Indian Ocean.

This is why it may be inappropriate to think of the Indian diaspora as forever an “outsider” population. For many of these families, Mozambique is not simply the country where they live. It is the country where they were born, where their parents were born, where their ancestors are buried, and where they built their lives. India may be their family origin. Mozambique is, for many, a homeland.
The ongoing question

Around half a century after independence, the question of nationality continues to be more than a matter of just documents. It is a question of recognition. Who has the right to say “I am Mozambican”? Is it enough to have been born in the country? Have Mozambican parents? Have lived in the country for decades? Participate in society? Speak its languages? Share a collective memory? Or will some people continue to be seen as foreigners by many, despite legally being citizens? It is in this space between the law and general perception that many identities exist.

This evokes the concept of a “bridge” — Mozambique’s Indian-origin community historically finds itself between different spaces: Africa and Asia, family tradition and national identity, migratory memory and territorial belonging. But being between two shores does not necessarily mean not belonging to either. Sometimes it means belonging to both. And, for some, it means discovering that their family history crossed oceans long before modern passports decided which country a person belonged to.

The history of Mozambique’s monhés is thus also a history about the very meaning of being Mozambican. Not a story of people who simply “came from outside,” but a story of people who, over generations, helped build the country, while continuing to negotiate, within their families and wider society the fundamental question that follows all those who migrate: where, in the end, is home?

003a6a0d932a932b: I think a lot about time. How we consume it, save it, enjoy it, spend it. How it can be interminably slow or rush by before you know it.

Our language subtly instructs us about our concept of time: We are urged to “savor the moment”; we want to “be present.” Even store clerks bid us to “have a good day”, as if you control whether this 24-hour period will be good or not. You can, of course, try your best to have a good day, and sometimes succeed – unless the universe has other plans for you.1
I’ve always been fascinated by time; maybe that’s why I was so intrigued by watches as a kid. A few recent events have me thinking about time more than usual: a big birthday, a loss, other events …
Age

I never had a midlife crisis. Perhaps it was too cliché. Big round birthdays and aging never bothered me. The only experience I had relative to age was waking up on the morning of my 60th birthday and immediately thinking, “Start of the fourth quarter, down by 7 – you’re still in this thing, but lots to do. Get busy!”

The result was a new book, some personal projects, financial and estate planning, and less procrastination on major purchases, travel, and activities I had been putting off for no good reason. As an immortal, I would get around to them eventually. Once the 19-year-old in me admitted immortality was no longer operative, I suddenly felt an urgency to check off some boxes. No, not a bucket list, just a short inventory of unfulfilled desires I suddenly felt the urge to make happen.
Hey, wait a second…
Impermanence
Our house developed an exterior leak that dripped into the basement. To prep for the contractors, we cleared out a lot of accumulated junk. The big surprise: 6 MacBooks dating back to the 2000s.

Six! Each one was a thing: expensive, useful, important, yet oh so temporary. We were warned: “Don’t throw away old laptops unless you removed the hard drives!” Looking at these old, battered MacBooks, I remember the excitement of buying them: Faster, better, improved! When we buy something new, we forget it will eventually wear out, get damaged, become less useful, get replaced or discarded. Everything!
The second law of thermodynamics is a bitch.
Illusion

Here’s something you might not have considered: Time, at least as an objective concept outside human consciousness, doesn’t exist. It’s (mostly) a human creation; no chrono particles, no celestial timekeeper, no physical mechanism governs time’s passage. Our experience is an illusion, a function of our sensory inputs colliding with our consciousness…

Physics recognizes Time is a useful construct, a handy artifice for comparing forces relative to one another. “T” in equations is time as a dimension between other vectors. You use it to measure speed or distance, but mostly relative to each other. Every measure of time seems to quantify only an object’s motion, whether it’s the vibration of a Cesium atom or the hands on a clock.2

I wonder: Does Time exist independently of us, conscious beings? Without us, does the relative motion of objects in 3-dimensional space include time – or is that simply a convenient human assumption? 3

The flow of time seems especially illusory: The sense of RIGHT HERE AND NOW, the intersection of THIS instant (T) and THIS location (X, Y, & Z), is moving forward, a present “now” that advances tick by tick, second by second, and millennia by millennia. I struggle to believe this is anything other than the human mind trying to make sense of the experiential universe…
Our experience of Time, which changes so radically over our lives, is an illusion.
Money is Time
I contributed a chapter to the new book “How I Invest My Money Volume Two,” which was published this week.
Excellent financial advice needs specific personalization; I wanted to write something universal. My chapter, titled “Money Is Time,” is a tight 860 words, but has three concepts worth sharing:
First, Money is society’s measure of the economic contributions you make with your time (including effort, expertise, insight, skill, etc., which are themselves functions of time).

Second, we all get precisely 24 hours a day. Each of us is born wealthy in time, with endless, infinite hours, days, weeks, months, and years, which we fritter away when young. Later in life, we learn that time is our stock in trade.

And third, Money IS Time. Every purchase you make is an investment of your insultingly limited time. The days may be long, but the decades are short. Keep this front of mind as you spend your finite supply of time.
Time Travel
As a sci-fi fan, I’ve sat through more than my fair share of time-travel flicks. Screenwriters and novelists seem to ignore two issues.

The first is Location: When you travel back in time, the planet you’re standing on will have moved – millions or billions of miles away. The Earth orbits the Sun at 66,600 mph; the Sun makes a 260-million-year route around the Milky Way at 515,000 mph; even the Earth’s rotation is 1,040 mph. You must surmise your position relative to the galactic expansion at 515,000 mph, despite its occasional changes in acceleration. 4

In total, we are moving at 828,000 mph. Time travel for a century, and you space travel 725 billion miles (best of luck calculating that precisely). Off by a trillionth of a %, e.g., ~three-quarters of a mile, you materialize inside Earth’s crust (deadly) or nearly 4,000 feet in the air before gravity ends you. Greater errors deliver you into the vacuum of space.

My second issue is the Arrow of Time. It annoys me to send people into a nondeterministic future that hasn’t happened yet. I don’t buy the thesis of a Universe as a block of past, present, and future all occurring at once – it lacks causality.5

In my version of time travel, you can go into the past, but only to return to the point from which you departed. But you cannot visit the Restaurant at the End of the Universe because it hasn’t happened yet. Between now and then, many things will shape what actually happens. But until then, the future doesn’t exist.6
Dog Time

People often think of their lives in terms of blocks of time: You lived in this house or apartment; you worked at this job or that one; you dated or married this person. These blocks make up the eras of your life.

I sometimes think of my life in terms of dogs: Erev was a Labrador retriever I had as a kid; Killer was the stray I adopted in college (and my dad fell in love with); when we moved out of the city, we rescued Max, a shepherd-bearded mutt puppy; Jackson was a Labradoodle who kept Max young until he was 17. Lexi (died young of encephalitis), then Kodie (who is 5), followed Jack. Teddy, a Portuguese Water Dog, followed Max. We had to say goodbye to him last week, and even though I knew it was coming, the grief still shocked me.

Dogs gauge time by how your scent slowly fades since you left the house. If you return at the ~same time every day, they approximate that by how your scent declines over the day. They know when you are returning by that marker.

We all lose friends and family; our relationships are complicated, filled with joy, angst, baggage, walls, and emotions. None of that complexity exists with dogs – they are pure, unconditional love; when they depart, the wound finds you naked and defenseless…
Optionality

As you get older, you begin to realize you kinda know how the movie ends: what you’ve accomplished, what you’ve earned, the people you affected, and who affected you. Not a full accounting, but a modest recognition of who you have become.

It begins to set: You realize what is increasingly unlikely to occur. Projects that might take 5, 10, or 20 years to reach fruition, learning a new language, starting a business, learning to read music, seem difficult to impossible.
That is the biggest disillusionment about aging: What you gain in agency, you lose in optionality.
1. Classic Yiddish expression: “Man plans, and God laughs…”

So, not really a thing on its own; if something only exists relative to an actual thing’s motion, does it really exist at all?

3. Einstein would argue that Relativity treats spacetime as a geometric object with four dimensions – X, Y, Z, and T. That distinction is probably the closest thing to Time as an objective entity independent of us, as anything else in physics.
I’m not sure how persuasive that is to me. Also, attempts to quantize gravity, such as the Wheeler-DeWitt equation, has no T. Time vanishes from the equations entirely

It’s an adequate Nobel Prize-winning theory, at least until a better one comes along.

0efd9cf003b3b02d: Gender diversity, resistance and ritual cross-dressing in Venezuela's sacred cult
Originally published on Global Voices

Portrait of Wander Rodríguez, part of the María Dolores Rodríguez Caravan and its powers, and the LGBTIQ+ community. Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.

In Venezuela, Spiritism as a religion is part of the collective imagination, of our identity; popular beliefs and ritual practices that take us back to our ancestors in colonial times. Over the years, Spiritism has evolved into a vibrant, contemporary national cult centered on the figure of María Lionza as the principal protector of waters and the charms of nature, a figure who challenges the notions of the patriarchal state and opposes monotheistic religions.

This religious system has been studied in depth by anthropologists in our country (Daisy Barreto, Angelina Pollak-Eltz, Michelle Asencio, Francisco Ferrándiz, Cesar Escalona, among others), which I had read about and found interesting at the time, but which I later witnessed for the first time in its most important sites, such as Quibayo and Sorte, in the state of Yaracuy, Venezuela.
Altar to María Lionza in Quibayo (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 11. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.

These sites are part of the Cerro María Lionza Natural Monument, popularly known as the Montaña de Sorte, and they represent the most prominent expressions of this cult nationwide, so they are visited year-round by practitioners or “caravans” (as these groups are commonly called),
But few days are as important as October 11 and 12, when thousands of people flock there to celebrate the Day of Indigenous Resistance in Venezuela.

These dates offer an opportunity for ethnographic and cultural observation, specifically how oral histories and our ethnic origins are reclaimed; including those of Indigenous peoples, some of them warriors who fought against Spanish colonization, and African populations — enslaved people and maroons — as we can understand through the figure of the Three Powers: Queen María Lionza as the central figure of the cult, the leader, accompanied by El Indio Guaicaipuro and El Negro Felipe.
Altar to Queen María Lionza in Quibayo (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 11. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.

For this celebration families gather among the trees and along the banks of the Yaracuy River, which runs through the entire mountain, setting up lavish altars to the various deities of Venezuelan spiritualism, which embody the sacred rituals characteristic of the Marialioncero cult.

The figure of María Lionza is profound, and I believe it is risky to oversimplify her, as she is regarded as a Queen, a Goddess, a mother, and a guardian, yet there are also aspects linked to her sensuality, as evidenced by the iconographic representations of her that have emerged -naked or clothed, for example-.

In this regard, I draw upon the writings of Francisco Ferrándiz and César Escalona from the perspective of Venezuelan anthropology, combining them with my own observations and field interviews, to address issues related to gender and sexual diversity that are essential to the fascinating debate within the cult on its various courts — such as the Black Court, the Viking Court, the Malandra Court, the Chamarrera Court, and the Medical Court, among others — and entities.
Detail of flowers and bottles of the Baile del vidrio (Glass Dance Ritual) in Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.
Gender diversity, gender discrimination

The Sorte Mountain is a setting where gender stereotypes are called into question, and I believe they undermine androcentric perspectives and rigid notions of masculinity and femininity found within Christianity, since the entities pose a challenge due to their wide spectrum in terms of strength, height, voice, attire, and other details of the mediums who embody them, as well as the particular characteristics of each spirit.
Strenght between banks and Viking Court entity. Baile del vidrio (Glass Dance Ritual) in Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.

In his ethnographies and writings, Ferrandíz offers interesting reflections on the body and masculinity in this religion, and how male mediums (from a position of stigmatized masculinity) resisted possession by female spirits, something that did not occur as frequently among female spiritualists.
That is why my encounter in Sorte with the María Dolores Rodríguez Caravan and its powers — led by Osmer Padrón and his godchildren — allowed me to also explore these aspects.
Osmer Padrón embodies the spirit of María Dolores. Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.

Osmer Padrón, Wander Rodríguez, and Jhonaiker Díaz are all male mediums that belong to the LGBTQ+ community, and are part of this caravan that channels female entities from the Black Court, such as María Dolores Rodríguez, Francisca Martínez, Rita Encarnación, and La Negra Tomasa; but in Osmer’s case, he also channels Mister Piter, a male entity from the Viking Court, a warrior and healer.

Wander tells me that in the LGBTQ+ spiritualist community, “there’s a lot of discrimination, both inside and outside the mountain [of Sorte], but Queen María Lionza is love and affection, and as many spiritual beings have said, we are all deeply cherished by her. We are here first and foremost to fulfill a mandate from Goddess and our Majesty María Lionza. Nothing else matters.”

Portraits of Jhonaiker Díaz (who works with the spirit of La Negra Tomasa) and José Rojas. They are part of the LGBTIQ+ community. Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.
Regarding the practice of channeling female entities from the Black Court, Rodríguez tells me:

Most of us spiritualists in the LGBTQ+ community dress up in dresses — or find ourselves transported into that state — not because we want to… Right now, there’s a lot of talk from people saying that men who want to be women channel Black Court entities just to wear dresses, but that’s not the case. When a spiritual entity is a woman or was a woman, she always seeks to be fully covered, to cover her breasts, and why? Because she feels exposed; she feels alive. There are many spiritual entities, such as the Negra I work with — who is Rita Encarnación Martínez Chávez — as well as María Dolores Rodríguez Rodríguez, Francisca Martínez Martínez, and Negra Tomasa, who have their dresses made for them. It’s not because we want to wear dresses; if they were our own bodies, we’d walk around shirtless, but no, they always… Spirituality always seeks to feel alive; that’s why they put on their dress, their turban, and some even seek out a flower.

Dresses for female entities from the Black Court: Francisca Martínez, Francisca Palacios, María Dolores Rodríguez, Negra Tomasa and Rita Encarnación. Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.

There are curious details regarding what the entities ask of their “banks” —people who also care for the physical forms of the entities — such as tobacco and aguardiente; but in the case of the black women, just as they ask for their dresses, they also ask for makeup and make gestures as if looking at themselves in a mirror.

Wander tells me that, in the case of Rita Encarnación, “her favorite flower is the cayena, since it was the flower with which she learned to perform her magic, while she labels “other flowers as hypocrites, since those other flowers remain alive for many days after being plucked from nature, whereas the cayena once plucked from nature wilt immediately.”
Altar to Las Tres Potencias (The Three Powers), in Quibayo (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 11. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.

All of this demonstrates that Venezuelan spiritism must be examined through a gender lens, from a feminist perspective, reflecting on the power dynamics established between men and women, the presence of ritual cross-dressing during trance and possession rituals, and other aspects that enrich our understanding of this important Venezuelan religion.
Wander Rodríguez enters a trance to receive the spirit of Rita Encarnación. Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.
Written by Freisy González
7c2863bae5f69e0c: From Hartini Zainudin
Last Thursday, a newborn boy was found alive in a box under the stairs of a Kepong apartment block. The next morning, a baby girl was found dead in a rubbish bin at a Bangsar waste site.
Police are investigating the first case under Section 317 of the Penal Code for abandonment of a child, and the second under Section 318 for concealment of birth.
Two babies, found a day and a few kilometres apart. One will grow up as a foundling, the other never got that chance.
I have spent much of my working life between these two outcomes: recovering abandoned babies, sitting with mothers once they are traced, and raising children of my own through adoption.
These cases share a root, and we keep refusing to name it.
Infanticide begins long before the birth

The women, family and community development ministry recorded 72 baby dumping cases in 2025 and 18 in the first quarter of 2026. Selangor alone logged 43 last year. These are only the babies we know about. Concealed births and deaths that never reach the police sit outside every statistic.

Our law already accepts that infanticide differs from murder. Section 309A of the Penal Code applies when a mother causes the death of her newborn while her mind is disturbed by childbirth. Legislators wrote that provision because they understood something our public conversation still ignores: women in these cases are usually in crisis themselves.

In my experience, they are young — often teenagers — and have hidden the pregnancy for months, sometimes even from themselves. They have seen no doctor and give birth alone, in a bathroom or a hostel room, in pain and terror.

Some of them became pregnant through rape or incest by someone in the same house. Some are migrant workers who know a pregnancy can cost them a permit, a job and a roof in the same week. By the time the baby arrives, months of silence have done their work. Panic does the rest.
We respond by hunting for them. A police appeal goes out, the comment sections demand the harshest punishment, and every other frightened girl in Malaysia learns one lesson: better to hide.
The boy in Kepong survived the box. He now faces a slower danger.

The Federal Constitution was written with children like him in mind. Section 19B of Part III of the Second Schedule presumes that a newborn found abandoned was born here to a mother who is a permanent resident.

Section 1(e) of Part II makes anyone born in Malaysia who is not a citizen of any other country a citizen by operation of law. Together, they are meant to ensure that no abandoned child in Malaysia grows up stateless.

In 2024, the government proposed amendments that would have weakened both protections. Civil society, including many of us who worked with foundlings for decades, pushed back hard, and those changes were withdrawn before the bill passed. The safeguards stand.

Where they fail is in practice. Foundlings still leave hospitals with undetermined citizenships. Families who adopt them wait years for documents. Some children reach school age, then adulthood, unable to prove what the constitution already says they are.
What that does to a child

A foundling without citizenship pays foreigner rates at government hospitals. He may struggle to sit for public examinations, apply for a scholarship, open a bank account, marry legally or register the birth of his own children. Statelessness travels down generations.
He also carries the story. Adopted and fostered children eventually ask where they came from, and the answer begins with a box, a drain or a surau doorstep.

What we owe that child is a life in which that beginning does not decide everything that follows: a name, a nationality, a family and a fair start. Whether he gets them depends on paperwork handled by adults he will never meet.
The education we keep postponing
Almost every case I have handled traces back to the same gap.
A girl who does not understand her own body cannot recognise a pregnancy early. A girl who has never been told that what her uncle or stepfather does to her is abuse, does not know she can report it.
A boy who has never learned about consent does not see himself as responsible. A young woman who has never heard of confidential health services does not know which door to walk through.
Malaysian schools do teach reproductive health, but too often it is diluted, rushed or delivered only as a moral warning, by teachers who were never trained to teach it.
Young people end up learning about sex from friends and online, and learning about pregnancy too late.

International evidence, including Unesco's reviews of sexuality education programmes, shows that age-appropriate education does not make young people more sexually active. It helps them delay sex, protect themselves, and recognise and report abuse.
For a girl living with incest, knowing the words for what is happening to her can be the difference between a police report and a hidden pregnancy.
What must change
Comprehensive, age-appropriate sexuality and consent education in every school, taught by trained teachers, with parents brought in from the start.
Confidential crisis pregnancy care inside the public health system, so a girl can deliver safely in hospital and relinquish her baby lawfully without being treated as a suspect.
A welfare-first protocol: a mother who is traced sees a doctor and a social worker before a police investigating officer.
Automatic citizenship for every foundling at birth registration: apply Sections 19B and 1(e) as written. No child should need a lawyer or an NGO to claim what the constitution already guarantees.
Track the survivors: where foundlings are placed, whether they are adopted, and whether they ever receive a MyKad.
A name

This week, a welfare department officer will choose a name for the boy from Kepong. It will go on a form beside a blank space where his mother's name should be. Whether the line below it reads "warganegara" is up to us.
The baby girl from Bangsar will need a name too, for a grave.

Both were failed long before they were found: by classrooms that stayed silent, clinics their mothers did not know they could enter, and a system that protects foundlings on paper and abandons them in practice.
We know where the failures are. We have known for years.
Hartini Zainudin is co-founder of Yayasan Chow Kit, founder of Kasih Madhya, and co-founder of Voice of the Children.

1a30c83a19add1c9: From P Kamalanathan
Last week, during a visit to AIMST University, I met a Form 5 student. He was accompanying his sister to enroll in the university.
The Form 5 student was a straight As student.
When I asked about his ambition, he looked down and said: "Datuk, I am tired."
He is not alone.

The National Health and Morbidity Survey (NHMS) tells us a painful truth: 26.9% of our students aged 13 to 17 suffer from depressive disorders, while 13.1% have had suicidal thoughts, and 9.5% have attempted suicide.
Let me repeat: One in four is depressed. One in 10 has tried to end his/her life.
When I was deputy education minister, overseeing five million students, we worried about UPSR and SPM results.
Today, the Ipsos 2025 survey shows 37% of Malaysian parents worry about their children's mental health more than academic quality, and even more than bullying or social media.
Our children are not failing exams. We are failing to see they are hurting.

Last year, the education ministry recorded 7,681 bullying cases, up from 6,528 the year before. Pisa 2025 reported 27% of Malaysian students are bullied several times a month, higher than the OECD average of 20%.
A Monash study found 16% experience cyberbullying. Behind every statistic is a child who goes to the toilet and cries alone.
The recent tragic incidents in Petaling Jaya and Kedah shocked the nation. But let us be honest: tightening security and installing CCTV alone will not heal trauma, shame, isolation and fear.
What we need is a shift from report cards to "wellbeing cards".
Our new National Education Plan 2026-2035 speaks rightly of Karamah Insaniah, or human dignity. Dignity does not mean only respect for others. It means teaching a child to respect his own mind.
That is why I wish to propose three urgent actions:
1. Make mental health screening routine, not reactive.
We screen eyesight, we screen BMI. Why not mental health?

Studies by Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia (UKM) have shown that more than 60% of students show mild symptoms of depression, anxiety or stress, but only 33% are in the normal range. If we catch such symptoms early, we can save a life.
Schools should have biannual wellbeing screenings, which are confidential and conducted by trained counsellors, not discipline teachers.
2. Fix the counsellor ratio and protect their time.
Today one counsellor serves 500 students. How can one person listen to 500 stories?

A counsellor, teacher and friend, who has served for over 20 years in a secondary school, told me recently: "Datuk, we are not short of caring teachers. We are short of time. One teacher cannot be discipline warden, SPM marker, and counsellor all at once."

She explained that in schools, Saringan Minda Sihat is already conducted twice a year. Students identified as critical need counselling sessions and follow-up screening to see whether there is improvement.
So when many students need follow-up, the current counsellor ratio is definitely not enough.

She added that counsellors are not only handling mental health but also have to manage 'murid cicir' (dropouts), Ziarah Cakna (home visits), leadership programmes, vape, smoking and drug issues, character development, career education, UPU, PKSK, career pathways, tracking SPM and STPM leavers, and parent conferences, etc.
She strongly believes that counsellors need more protected time and a better counsellor-student ratio. I agree. She also suggested separating counselling from discipline duties.
We must aim for a ratio of 1:250 in urban schools and 1:200 in high-risk schools.
The HEAL Line 15555 by the health ministry has received 267,873 calls. That shows children want to talk. But they want to talk to someone they see daily, not a voice on the phone.
3. Build peer support, not just punishment.

Selangor's PeerZ model and Monash's Thrive Together 2026 initiative show that when students are trained to support each other, help-seeking increases. The Anti-Bullying Tribunal and Anti-Bullying Act 2026 are important for justice, but peer support is important for healing.
In Sentul where I grew up, my mother taught me: "Education without empathy is just information."
We have become excellent at providing information. We must now become excellent at providing empathy.
I told that Form 5 boy who I met at AIMST: Being tired is not failure. Tired is a signal. Like fever signals infection, tiredness signals you need rest, talk, help.
This Deepavali, we will light lamps outside. Let us also light lamps inside our children's minds. Do not ask your child, "What marks did you get?" but instead, ask "How did you feel today?"
Because a nation that produces straight As students but loses them to depression has not succeeded. It has failed.
P Kamalanathan is a former deputy education minister and an adjunct professor of Unitar International University.

68b8fa9b95dac59e: From Wan Agyl Wan Hassan
Malaysia’s debate over minimum e-hailing fares is about more than the price of a ride.
This raises a fundamental question: how do we protect drivers’ livelihoods without making everyday mobility more expensive for the public?
E-hailing has changed how Malaysians travel. It offers convenience, flexible earning opportunities and an important transport option in areas where conventional public transport remains inadequate.
For some commuters, it also provides the crucial connection between home and the nearest rail station.
Yet behind that convenience is an economic imbalance that deserves attention.

Drivers bear much of the cost of providing the service. Fuel, maintenance, insurance, financing and vehicle depreciation come out of their pockets. They also absorb the cost of travelling to pick-up points, returning without passengers and waiting between bookings.
These are legitimate concerns. However, increasing the minimum passenger fare does not necessarily resolve them.
What passengers pay and what drivers actually earn are not the same thing.
Consider two drivers. One completes a RM12 journey but waits another 45 minutes for the next booking.
Another completes two RM8 journeys over a similar period with little waiting time.
Depending on distance and operating expenses, the second driver could earn more despite charging less per trip.

This illustrates why driver welfare cannot be measured by individual fares alone. What matters is how much a driver retains after expenses and how many productive hours they achieve throughout the working day.
Our research into Malaysia’s e-hailing economy highlights the financial pressures faced by drivers.
Based on our operating-cost model, running a Perodua Bezza for e-hailing services costs approximately RM0.40 per kilometre, including fuel, maintenance, insurance and vehicle depreciation.
While this is an indicative estimate rather than an industry-wide benchmark, our findings highlight an important reality: drivers continue to incur costs even when they are not carrying passengers.
Travelling to pick-up points, repositioning between bookings and waiting for the next journey all affect their actual take-home earnings.
This is why proposals for a minimum base fare, distance tariff and time-based compensation require careful examination.

A five-kilometre journey through Kuala Lumpur during evening congestion is very different from a similar journey on a free-flowing suburban road. The distance may be identical, but the time commitment and opportunity to secure subsequent bookings are not.
Conditions also differ outside major cities, where drivers may face longer waiting periods and fewer passengers.
A uniform national fare formula could therefore benefit some drivers while disadvantaging others.
Without reliable information on actual operating costs, trip demand and driver utilisation, setting a statutory rate risks creating new problems even as it attempts to solve existing ones.
There is also the passenger to consider.

For many Malaysians, e-hailing is not a luxury. It is a practical transport option, particularly where buses are infrequent, rail stations are difficult to reach or travelling without a private vehicle is inconvenient.
In Greater Kuala Lumpur, some commuters depend on e-hailing for short journeys to MRT and LRT stations.
If that connection becomes disproportionately expensive, the entire public transport journey becomes less attractive.
Some may return to driving or riding motorcycles. Others may simply travel less.
Neither outcome should be dismissed when Malaysia is investing heavily in improving public transport accessibility.
However, affordable feeder services should not come at the expense of drivers.
If the government wants to encourage first- and last-mile connectivity, targeted subsidies, integrated ticketing and demand-responsive transit should be considered.
Drivers should not be expected to absorb the cost of achieving national public transport objectives.
This brings us to the more important regulatory question: should Malaysia focus on setting minimum passenger fares or protecting minimum driver earnings?

The Gig Workers Act 2025 provides an opportunity to examine this distinction. Through the Gig Workers’ Consultative Council, Malaysia now has a statutory mechanism for considering minimum earnings rates and formulas appropriate to different categories of gig work.

Rather than immediately imposing a uniform passenger fare floor, policymakers should examine whether minimum driver remuneration, supported by reasonable expense recovery, would offer more direct protection.

Such an approach must also address unpaid working time such as dead mileage. Protecting earnings only while a passenger is onboard may still leave drivers exposed to long periods of uncompensated waiting.

Platform accountability is equally important. Malaysia already has commission ceilings for e-hailing services, but regulators must ensure that deductions are transparent, existing requirements are enforced and drivers understand how their earnings are calculated.
Reducing commission ceilings may appear attractive, but its effects on platform viability, incentives, competition and passenger prices must also be assessed.

The wider institutional framework deserves attention. Transport regulation, worker protection and competition oversight involve different authorities. Whether Malaysia strengthens existing institutions or establishes additional regulatory arrangements, responsibilities must be clear and enforcement effective.
Creating another regulatory body will not automatically improve driver earnings if the underlying economic problems remain unresolved.

Before introducing binding fare formulas, Malaysia needs a credible assessment of driver operating costs, actual take-home earnings, unpaid mileage, working hours, platform deductions and passenger affordability.
The findings should guide regulation, not the other way around.

Drivers deserve fair remuneration for their time, effort and investment. Passengers deserve affordable and reliable mobility. Platforms need sustainable commercial conditions, while regulators must protect the wider public interest.
These objectives need not conflict, but achieving them requires evidence rather than assumptions.

Malaysia should not confuse higher fares with better livelihoods. The true measure of successful e-hailing regulation is whether drivers earn a reasonable return, passengers can still afford to travel and the transport system continues to serve both.
That is the equilibrium worth pursuing.
Wan Agyl Wan Hassan is the founder and senior adviser to MY Mobility Vision, a transport think tank.

52bd68910fc3a807: Sabah and Sarawak have long been touted as examples of what Malaysian unity is supposed to look like. We are told that in these two states, people of various faiths and races live together effortlessly.
Apparently, everyone in East Malaysia celebrates each other’s festivals as a family. There are no reservations among those of different faiths or suspicions that one group is out to get another.
I am told that in Sabah and Sarawak, people of different races even sit at the same table in a coffeeshop.
This scenario harkens back to a time when Malay Muslims in the peninsula were not as conservative as they are nowadays — a time when they were more relaxed and would mix well with other Malaysians.
That is in stark contrast to the Taliban-like mentality we encounter these days.
Unfortunately, it seems religious and racial parochialism may have now arrived on Sabah and Sarawak’s shores.
A Sarawakian MP’s concern about primary schoolers not wanting to sit next to pork-consuming or crucifix-wearing classmates is the most damning proof that conservatism has set foot in East Malaysia.
In truth, religious conservatism did not appear in East Malaysia overnight.

I do recall the controversy over plans to construct a statue of Mazu, the Chinese goddess of the sea, which was abandoned in 2006 following objections by the Muslim community on the grounds that the site was too near the town mosque.
In 2024, a petrol bomb was thrown at a KK Mart outlet in Kuching in the wake of the “Allah” socks controversy.
And just last month, there was an uproar over a concert by US gospel singer Israel Houghton, with his name and stance on Israel triggering sensitivities within the community.
How did this come to be? A change in demographics?

Sure, Sabah and Sarawak’s Malay population may have increased. Even so, the community's attitude towards religion remains considerably more tolerant than that of its counterparts in Peninsular Malaysia.
But I blame the rapid spread of technology, especially the internet and social media.
Extremist views and fiery rhetoric can now be accessed around the clock, fuelling hatred and poisoning the younger generation.
Strict immigration controls are powerless against the digital penetration of extremist ideologies and divisive rhetoric.
Sabah and Sarawak risk losing their status as the last bastion of the Malaysian way of life envisioned by our forefathers.

At the risk of being ridiculed for saying so, I fear that within the next decade the two states could become just as consumed by racial and religious rhetoric as parts of Peninsular Malaysia are today.
But, despite my pessimistic outlook, all is not lost, yet.
The two East Malaysia states must look into retraining teachers of religion and history — two subjects that must integrate aspects of nation building.
History must be taught in a more inclusive manner: the contributions of every race and tribe should be acknowledged when speaking about the state and country’s development.
After all, there is a wealth of evidence to show how all races and faiths have contributed to Malaysia’s growth.
It is just a matter of having these contributions documented, preferably by a group of honest Malaysians who believe in the idea of a true Malaysia for all.
There are also ways to weave the values Islam teaches into the Rukun Negara while educating Muslims on how to coexist in a plural society.
Sabah and Sarawak have shown their autonomous streak in recognising the Unified Examination Certificate. Sarawak uses English alongside Bahasa Malaysia for official purposes.
The two states should likewise use their autonomy to counter the growing influence of narrow and divisive worldviews.
Sabah and Sarawak stand as the final bastion of the Malaysian ideal envisioned by our forefathers, one built on mutual respect, coexistence and shared progress.
Sadly, Peninsular Malaysia is a lost cause since the malady it suffers from cannot be treated without severe backlash.
But if Sabah and Sarawak dilly-dally on this issue, even they will not escape the threats that race and religious extremism can bring.
And, this time, we won’t be able to pin the blame on politicians.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
50156b4defde56fe: Kita kini berdepan dengan moraliti baharu. Biasanya seseorang yang didapati bersalah atau kalah saman maka pihak itu dikatakan kalah dan tidak berada dalam kebenaran moral. Namun demikian, perkara terbalik kini mungkin terjadi apabila pihak kalah dilihat sebagai mangsa penghakiman dan ia juga dilihat sebagai pejuang kaum atau agama. Saya akan membentangkan dua kajian kes dalam hal ini.

Kajian kes pertama adalah kes saman Teresa Kok daripada DAP ke atas Dr Akmal Saleh daripada Umno yang berakhir dengan kemenangan mahkamah kepada Kok dengan perintah supaya Akmal membayar RM300,000. Manakala kes kedua adalah saman Kok, Lim Kit Siang dan Lim Guan Eng ke atas Siti Mastura Muhammad daripada PAS yang berakhir dengan perintah mahkamah supaya wakil rakyat PAS itu membayar RM850,000. Jelas dalam satu perspektif DAP menang 2-0 dan PAS serta Umno tewas teruk. Namun, bagaimana pula perspektif politik? Ini yang menarik, tuan-tuan. Dalam bacaan saya DAP kalah 0-2 manakala PAS menang 1-0 dan Umno menang 1-0. Pelik kan? Tak juga, ia adalah politik ala Melayu.

Dalam kes pertama, Akmal didapati bersalah menghina Kok sehingga menyifatkan beliau sebagai musuh Islam. Kita semua dengan jelas dapat membaca sendiri kata-kata kasar Akmal dengan penggunaan ‘nyonya tua’ serta nak bagi cop halal pada dahinya. Hakim mahkamah telah menyimpulkan Akmal bertindak di luar daripada adab perbezaan pendapat dan debat politik kepada sesuatu yang membahayakan masyarakat, sefaham saya. Maka, Akmal diperintahkan membayar Kok RM300,000.

Maka, timbullah keesokannya gambar Akmal dengan nada sedih duduk termenung depan kolam ikan tilapianya sambil mengungkap untuk menjual motosikal dan ikannya melalui lelongan supaya dapat membayar Kok. Diberitakan hanya beberapa jam sahaja beliau dapat mengutip lebih RM40,000 ke dalam akaun peribadinya. Namun demikian, beliau berkeras tidak mahu orang menderma dan masih mahu menjalankan lelongannya seperti dibuat oleh sahabat Umno lain, Jamal Yunos. Kok nampaknya meraih banyak kekayaan dengan samannya yang lumayan. Jadi, soalannya bagaimana pula dikatakan DAP kalah politik dan Umno menang pula dalam hal ini? Sabar, tuan-tuan, kita ulas kes kedua pula.

Dalam kajian kes kedua, kita berdepan dengan kenyataan Mastura yang memfitnah Guan Eng dan Kit Siang sebagai sepupu kepada Lee Kuan Yew. Walaupun jelas pangkal nama Lim dan Lee berbeza entah macam mana seorang yang bergelar PhD tidak faham akan nama orang Cina. Bila dituduh memfitnah, Mastura mengemukakan ‘bukti’ daripada buku kempen Barisan Nasional. Tetapi, oleh kerana buku itu tiada nama penulis maka sukar untuk dibawa bukti kerana tiada badan yang nak menjawab. Mastura sepatutnya tidak meletakkan kredibiliti yang tinggi kepada suatu sumber yang memang tugasnya berperang politik. Dalam peperangan, anything goes asalkan menang. Maka, menanglah orang DAP dan Mastura berdepan pembayaran yang bukan kepalang sedikit; hampir RM1 juta. Nasib baik, PAS menggerakkan partinya dengan membuat gerakan ‘derma jihad’ pada keseluruhan jentera. Surat yang ditulis seperti tidak mengaku kesalahan tetapi membuat episod itu sebagai ‘perjuangan Islam’. Maka, dalam kurang lebih seminggu, wang sejumlah banyak itu dapat dikutip dan terus diserahkan kepada pihak peguam. Memang PAS cukup hebat dan saya pun mengagumi parti tersebut yang berjaya mengutip dengan pantas. Hari ini, dah lebih satu bulan, wang RM50 juta belum siap Umno kutip lagi, dan entah bila Najib Razak dapat pulang ke pangkuan keluarga. Jadi, soalannya bagaimana pula dikatakan yang DAP kalah politik dan PAS menang pula?

Begini, saya lihat moral orang Islam dan Melayu daripada kajian kes kedua-duanya. Dalam kes Akmal, penyokong Umno dan Akmal yang saya anggap semuanya Melayu tidak mempunyai pandangan bahawa ada kesalahan pun apabila Akmal bercakap kasar dan membuatkan Kok seperti seorang musuh Islam. Ramai orang Melayu sudah selesa dengan naratif DAP musuh Melayu dan Islam, jadi tidaklah surprise, yang penyokong Akmal masih menganggap Akmal sebagai the hero dan Kok sebagai the villain. Dunia dah terbalik agaknya di mana yang mengasari dianggap betul dan yang dikasari dianggap tidak betul. Jadi, apabila lelongan atau derma kilat kepada Akmal mungkin terkutip dalam kurang lebih seminggu, kita akan mendapat satu moraliti politik yang baharu bahawa untuk berjuang kita kena kasar dan menuduh sebarang apa pun as long as it works. Itu nampaknya adab baharu dalam politik Melayu. Jadi, sah Akmal lagi popular dan Kok serta DAP lagi lebih dibenci Melayu. So, Akmal menang, Kok kalah dalam politik 'Malaysia boleh'.

Dalam kajian kes kedua, terdapat moral lebih berat lagi yang diterima pakai oleh orang Melayu. Dengan bukti cepatnya koleksi ‘derma jihad’ maka jihad Islam dah masuk menyokong fitnah yang disahkan pengadilan mahkamah dan pengadilan umum. Tetapi, oleh kerana sayangnya Melayu kepada agama Islam dan parti yang menempik sebagai pejuang nombor wahid Islam maka fitnah kepada orang bukan Islam seperti macam tak ada nilai langsung dari aspek dosa dan pahala. Malah, silap hari bulan membantu mangsa saman DAP mungkin dianggap mendapat pahala dengan menderma wang ringgit yang sepatutnya boleh diberi makan anak beranak atau fakir miskin. Ini bukan sahaja suatu evolusi moral Melayu tetapi ia melangkaui kepada nilai Islam; menyokong fitnah untuk membantu perjuangan Islam. Oleh yang demikian saya membuat deklarasi bahawa PAS-Mastura menang dan DAP bertiga kalah dalam politik ala Islam di Malaysia.

Paling menarik juga bagi saya, kes Jamal tidak mendapat bantuan daripada penyokong Umno maka beliau kekal tewas mahkamah dan tewas politik Melayu sebab tiada derma kilat untuknya. Nampaknya, setelah 40 tahun saya mengikuti politik Islam di Malaysia, baru kini saya dapat lihat perkembangan moral ‘Islam’ baharu didikan dua parti besar Melayu. Syabaslah saya ucapkan.
Artikel ini adalah pandangan penulis dan tidak semestinya mewakili FMT.
67e50ee91b5fe7cd: From Tunku Azizah Aminah Maimunah Iskandariah
Bismillahirrahmanirrahim.
Assalamualaikum warahmatullahi wabarakatuh, and a very good morning.
Distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen,

Before Tun Abdul Razak Hussein became the Prime Minister, he was already a Shahbandar. Before the nation entrusted him with its government, the Sultan of Pahang had entrusted him with an office rooted in our history.

We know much about what Tun Razak gave to Malaysia. Today, I would like us to consider what Pahang had given to Tun Razak. The family into which he was born. The office to which he was appointed. The traditions of government, adab and service that formed part of his world.
My subject today is the Shahbandar: his place beside the ruler, his responsibilities towards the people, and the amanah that gave his title meaning.
Through that history, I hope we may come to see a familiar man more fully. And I hope we will also look afresh at the history of government in our own country.
'Man Who Walked the Talk'

On Oct 9, I attended a screening of "Man Who Walked the Talk: The Tun Razak Story". As I watched, my thoughts returned to the Hukum Kanun Pahang. I had spent so much time studying its account of government and the responsibilities of those who assisted the ruler.
Then the connection struck me. Tun Razak was the tenth Orang Kaya Indera Shahbandar. The Shahbandar had become Prime Minister.

In an interview afterwards, I said, “It is in their blood, from one generation to another.” By that, I meant a legacy of service: knowledge learned at home, responsibilities observed at close quarters and an understanding of government cultivated across generations.
The person who later entered national politics had already grown up within a tradition of public responsibility.

To understand that tradition, we must look beyond the borders and institutions familiar to us today. The seas of the Malay world connected people. Across them travelled merchants, scholars, craftsmen, families and those seeking a new home.

Bugis migration and maritime activity were part of that movement. By the late 17th and early 18th centuries, Bugis communities and leaders had become an increasingly important presence in the western Malay world.

Their political influence became especially significant in the Johor–Riau world in 1722. They entered a political world with older roots in Melaka and Johor. Through alliances, marriage, trade and service, they helped shape its subsequent history, including the interconnected histories of Johor, Pahang, Riau and Lingga. Within that wider story lies the history of the Shahbandar family.
Family succession

The family genealogy records a connection through the female line to To’ Tuan, a Bugis chief associated with settlement in Pahang around 1722 and improvements in silk weaving. To’ Tondek appears as the first Shahbandar in the recorded family succession.

The settlement date should not be mistaken for a securely established date of first appointment. But it places the family’s connections within a history extending back about three centuries. Of the twelve holders in the succession we are discussing, eleven have belonged to the same family. There was an intervening appointment outside it.
Tun Razak was the tenth. His son, Najib, became the 11th. His grandson, Nizar, is the 12th. The family continuity is remarkable. Yet the office has always demanded more than a place in a genealogy.
Pahang was a vast kingdom. Its mountains, forests, river valleys and coastal settlements presented very different demands.

A ruler needed trusted people through whom the affairs of the country could be conducted. He needed knowledge of places and communities, counsel he could consider and officers able to carry out their responsibilities. The Orang Besar Berempat formed part of that structure.

The Orang Kaya Indera Perba Jelai was associated with Jelai; the Orang Kaya Indera Segara with Temerloh; the Orang Kaya Indera Pahlawan with Chenor; and the Orang Kaya Indera Shahbandar with Pekan. Each had regional responsibilities. Together, their offices helped sustain government across Pahang.

The Shahbandar’s proximity to the capital gave his office a particular importance. Generations of Shahbandars have served Pahang’s rulers, offering counsel and assisting in government according to the responsibilities of their time. As my husband reminded me when we discussed this subject, the Shahbandar worked closely with the Sultan.
Linehan observed that the Shahbandar’s position near the capital tended to make him the ruler’s manteri, or chief executive officer. In that sense, he was the ruler’s right-hand man.
Such proximity carried obligations. A trusted officer needed to understand the ruler’s concerns, offer considered advice and help translate decisions into action.

The title placed him within the working life of the palace and the affairs of the state. It was an office with work to do. My study of the Hukum Kanun Melaka and Hukum Kanun Pahang helped me recognise the historical importance of the Shahbandar.
Traditions of administration

Our history of government did not begin in 1957. Long before independence, Malay-Islamic kingdoms possessed their own institutions, offices, laws and traditions of administration. These developed according to the circumstances of their lands, their people and their faith.

The Sultan governed with the assistance of appointed officers. Responsibilities were distributed. Authority carried obligations. The relationship between ruler, ministers and people was a subject of thought, instruction and law. We had written these things down.

In the Hukum Kanun Melaka and Hukum Kanun Pahang, we encounter a civilisation articulating how it should be governed. These texts deserve to be studied as evidence of an indigenous understanding of government, with its own intellectual and Islamic foundations.

In my reading of the Hukum Kanun Pahang, the Shahbandar’s role is articulated: the qualities expected of him, his conduct, his responsibilities and the amanah entrusted to him. The office had expectations that its holder was required to fulfil.

Within a family, the younger generation could learn through observation and guidance how to meet those expectations. The text articulated the responsibilities; upbringing could help make them part of a person’s conduct.

The earlier legal office and the later Orang Kaya Indera Shahbandar belong to different stages of history. Their powers and circumstances were not identical. But both invite us to ask how people were prepared to exercise authority in service to the ruler and the country.

This is why the Shahbandar family interests me. Administration was a longstanding part of its history. Its connection with government preceded Tun Razak’s national political career. To understand him as a Shahbandar is to recognise a family tradition of administrators, and to ask how its experience could help prepare a later generation for public responsibility.

How does someone learn such a role? Part of the answer lies in education that does not begin with a school timetable. A son watches his father receive visitors. He hears matters of the state being discussed. He observes how advice is offered, how requests are answered and how the ruler is approached.

Some lessons are deliberately taught. Others are absorbed through the life of the household. There is informal learning through daily observation. There is also more deliberate instruction outside school: guidance in custom, protocol and the duties associated with office. Across generations, the role can be shaped, taught and practised in this way.

Palace protocol was part of the culture of such a family. The order of precedence, respect for seniority, when to stand, when to bow and how to address the ruler could be learned through observation, correction and repeated participation. These things did not have to wait for a formal lesson when a person entered public office. They belonged to the world in which the family lived.

In my view, this helps us understand an additional advantage in Tun Razak’s preparation: familiarity with the conduct expected in formal settings. That grounding could serve him at home and abroad, even as international diplomacy brought its own conventions to learn.
Protocol also teaches attentiveness: knowing who is present, understanding the occasion and showing consideration to others.

The prestige of the title carried expectations. A child raised within that tradition could learn what the position required: how to behave, how to carry himself and how to exercise authority with dignity and restraint.

The role itself could shape the person, even before he was called upon to fulfil it. Its responsibilities could become deeply ingrained through upbringing, rather than appearing for the first time on the day of appointment.

Receiving foreign dignitaries was another setting in which familiarity with courtly conduct could be useful. Knowing how to welcome a guest, recognise seniority and uphold the dignity of an occasion mattered within the palace. Such habits could also help a man who would later represent Malaysia internationally as Prime Minister.

I recognise something of this in a royal family. A prince begins learning the art of kingship before he ascends the throne. He observes his father listening, weighing advice and carrying the responsibilities of the Crown.
A future Shahbandar could receive a similar preparation for service. From father to son, and from elders to the younger generation, a body of experience could be carried forward. That is a legacy.
That is what I meant when I said, “It is in their blood.”
I was speaking of something deeply ingrained through upbringing and example. Of course, an upbringing cannot guarantee the quality of a person’s conduct.

Just as rulers must be judged by how they fulfil their responsibilities, so must Shahbandars. Within any tradition, there is the possibility of good leadership and poor leadership, of duty fulfilled and duty neglected. Every generation must answer for its own actions. An ancestor’s service is an example to follow. The descendant still has to do the work.

Tun Razak's father, Dato’ Hussein, was himself the Orang Kaya Indera Shahbandar and served as District Officer of Bentong. The family’s experience therefore included both a traditional office and work within the administrative service.
Knowledge and experience

Tun Razak was also blessed with the opportunity for formal education. He attended the Malay College Kuala Kangsar and Raffles College in Singapore, and later trained in law at Lincoln’s Inn in London.

That education gave him further knowledge and experience with which to approach the demands of government. He encountered different institutions, legal reasoning and the political questions of his time. I find the meeting of these forms of education especially interesting.

The household could cultivate familiarity with duty, custom and the relationship between ruler and people. Schooling and legal training equipped him for other institutions and wider responsibilities. His formation drew upon both.

That family background also matters when we consider his entry into electoral politics. Umno’s own account describes the family as well respected among the people of Pekan. He came into public life with more than a curriculum vitae: he carried a family name and an office already familiar in the community.
For kampung people who knew that family, he could be recognised through an existing relationship with the place and its people. Such familiarity may have helped him gain a hearing and build support.

Its precise electoral effect would require closer study, but it is a reasonable part of the story to explore. A known name could open a door. He still had to earn the confidence of those he sought to represent.

His experience in rural Pahang matters here too. The biographical accounts place part of his childhood with his grandparents in a kampung setting. His formation included elders, local people and village life, as well as the family’s connection with the palace.

The family’s connection with weaving brings another dimension to this story. Accounts of To’ Tuan, also known as Keraing Aji, associate him with Kampung Mengkasar in Pekan and the improvement of local silk-weaving methods. Pulau Keladi, too, belongs in this wider history of weaving, and it was Tun Razak’s birthplace. The contribution from Sulawesi enriched a developing Pahang tradition. People brought skills, adapted them and passed them on.

My work with Tenun Pahang Di Raja has taught me how much knowledge lives in practice. A weaver learns by watching, asking and trying again. The pattern matters, but so does the judgment of the hands. I have also encountered Tenun Pahang Di Raja in the protection or binding of the Hukum Kanun Pahang manuscripts in my care.

For me, that association is deeply moving. The written heritage of government was preserved with the woven heritage of our people. The dates of the text and its cloth must be studied separately. But their association reminds me that preservation itself is an act of responsibility.
Someone made the cloth. Someone cared for the manuscript. Someone ensured that the next generation could receive them. That is how a legacy survives.
By royal appointment

There is one point I wish to make very clearly. The Orang Kaya Indera Shahbandar holds office by royal appointment of the Sultan of Pahang. A long family association can make an office hereditary in custom. It does not make succession automatic.

A child may be born into the family and raised with an awareness of its responsibilities. He is not born with an unconditional entitlement to the office. The appointment remains the ruler’s prerogative, exercised within the applicable constitutional and customary framework. The Sultan considers the person who is to be entrusted with that responsibility.
Family history has its place. So do character, qualifications, ability and the contribution a person can make. The Sultan’s responsibility in making that choice is therefore profound.

I think of the ruler as a gardener choosing the trees and plants that will help a garden flourish. He must consider their character, their suitability and what they will contribute to the whole. A gardener also tends what he has planted. In the same way, appointment calls for continuing attention to how responsibility is being fulfilled.

We can also picture the state as a house: the Sultan is its roof, and the ministers and officers are its supporting pillars. Each must perform its part if the house is to shelter those within it. A pillar must be strong enough to carry its responsibility. The choice of those who support the ruler therefore concerns the wellbeing of the people who depend upon good government.

Above all, this responsibility must be understood in relation to hukum Islam. In my reading of the Hukum Kanun Pahang, authority carries an amanah: to uphold justice, act honestly and exercise power responsibly. The education of a Shahbandar must reach into this moral understanding of office.

Protocol teaches how to stand before a ruler. Islamic principles guide how one should act towards every person entrusted to one’s care. Adab must be evident in receiving a foreign dignitary and in listening to a villager seeking help. The dignity of the office is tested in both encounters.

The Shahbandar’s service to the ruler and the people must therefore be guided by justice, integrity and the knowledge that he is accountable before Allah for the trust he carries. The Islamic understanding of humanity’s responsibility as khalifah on earth gives that trust its moral weight. The ruler and those who assist him must consider how their authority is exercised, whom it protects and whether it serves justice.

Our ancestors thought about these responsibilities deeply enough to preserve them in writing. We owe it to them, and to ourselves, to read and understand what they left us. The roof, the pillars and those who live beneath them all belong within that understanding of responsibility.

There is ceremony, too. The conferment of titles and the Istiadat Menjunjung Duli give public expression to the relationship between ruler and those appointed to serve. In Menjunjung Duli, the officeholder acknowledges allegiance and responsibility before the ruler. The ceremony should remain alive in the conduct that follows it.

I would therefore remind the holder of this distinguished office, and all those entrusted with similar responsibilities: remember the source of your appointment. You hold this office by the Sultan’s appointment. It is not an elected office, and family expectation alone does not confer it. Honour the confidence placed in you through your service, your judgement and your conduct.
To stand close to the ruler is to carry a serious trust.

Tun Razak held two offices that help us understand the journey I am describing. One placed him within Pahang’s longstanding tradition of service under the ruler. The other placed him at the head of the national government.

He belonged by birth to the Shahbandar family; he held the Shahbandar office by appointment. He later became Prime Minister through the constitutional processes of a modern nation. Both offices carried responsibilities, although their powers and foundations differed.

He became Shahbandar in 1950, Pahang State Secretary in 1952 and Menteri Besar in 1955. Before Merdeka in 1957, he had already served within the government of Pahang. His later service as Deputy Prime Minister and Prime Minister extended his responsibilities to the nation.
So what did Pahang contribute to Malaysia through him?

A leader with formal education and administrative experience, certainly. I would also invite us to consider the tradition of service in which he had been raised: a familiarity with the affairs of government, the responsibilities of office and the relationship between authority and obligation.
Continuity of experience and political culture
3fe4e5c815518549: Malaysia's express bus industry is facing a new regulatory burden that raises serious questions about competition, commercial freedom and the government's understanding of public transport.
On Oct 16, the transport minister approved a policy requiring all express bus tickets to be sold exclusively through licensed bus terminals.
The Land Public Transport Agency (Apad) director-general subsequently issued a circular directing operators to comply from Nov 1, 2026, giving the industry just over two weeks to prepare.
The implications are serious.

This is not merely a change in ticketing arrangements. It shifts control over ticket sales from bus operators to terminal operators, creating a new layer of commercial control over an industry already struggling with rising operating costs.
The first question is obvious: why should a terminal operator have the exclusive right to sell tickets for a bus service that it does not operate?
Would Malaysia Airlines and AirAsia allow KLIA, the airport operator, to become the exclusive seller of their tickets?
It would be interesting to hear the views of the airlines' owners and CEOs if the Civil Aviation Authority of Malaysia were to issue such a directive and require compliance within two weeks.
There is nothing unusual about terminal operators collecting terminal charges and passenger service fees. But granting them exclusive control over ticket sales is an entirely different matter.
The proposal is difficult to justify and has little precedent elsewhere.
Terminals should serve buses, not control their ticket sales.
Malaysia's express bus industry has long been constrained by a terminal-centric approach to public transport planning.
Operators are required to serve designated terminals regardless of whether those locations are convenient for passengers or adequately integrated with other transport services.
Many terminals have also evolved into commercial property ventures, backed by substantial investments in buildings and facilities that must generate returns.
Bus operators are expected to pay terminal charges, while passengers bear the inconvenience and additional cost of travelling to terminals that may be poorly connected to their actual destinations.
The situation becomes even more problematic when terminal operators are given exclusive control over ticket sales.

Under Apad's new directive, terminal operators will have the sole right to sell tickets for express bus services operating from their terminals. They will also assume responsibility for trip management, departures and ticket-sale transactions.

This raises another obvious question. If bus operators are responsible for running services, maintaining fleets, employing drivers and meeting safety requirements, why should they be required to surrender control of their own ticket sales?
A terminal provides infrastructure. A bus operator provides transport services.
These are distinct commercial functions. There is no compelling reason to combine them under a compulsory arrangement that gives one party control over the other's revenue stream.
The transport ministry should seriously reconsider Apad's directive before it takes effect.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
defc8a4c0a097cca: Industri bas ekspres negara kini berdepan satu lagi beban kawal selia yang menimbulkan persoalan besar mengenai persaingan, kebebasan komersial dan sejauh mana kerajaan memahami operasi sebenar pengangkutan awam.
Pada 16 Okt, Menteri Pengangkutan Loke Siew Fook mengumumkan dasar yang menetapkan semua tiket bas ekspres mesti dijual hanya melalui terminal bas berlesen.

Ketua pengarah Agensi Pengangkutan Awam Darat (Apad) kemudian mengeluarkan pekeliling mengarahkan pengusaha bas mematuhi ketetapan itu mulai 1 Nov 2026, sekali gus memberi mereka tempoh hanya lebih dua minggu untuk membuat persediaan.
Implikasinya bukan kecil.

Ini bukan sekadar perubahan dalam kaedah penjualan tiket. Ia memindahkan kawalan jualan tiket daripada pengusaha bas kepada pengendali terminal dan mewujudkan satu lagi lapisan kawalan komersial dalam industri yang sudah berdepan peningkatan kos operasi.
Persoalan paling asas ialah mengapa pengendali terminal perlu diberi hak eksklusif menjual tiket bagi perkhidmatan bas yang bukan mereka kendalikan?
Adakah Malaysia Airlines dan AirAsia akan bersetuju sekiranya pengendali KLIA diberi hak eksklusif menjual tiket penerbangan mereka?

Menarik juga untuk mengetahui reaksi pemilik dan CEO syarikat penerbangan sekiranya Pihak Berkuasa Penerbangan Awam Malaysia mengeluarkan arahan sedemikian dan memberi tempoh hanya dua minggu untuk dipatuhi.

Tiada apa yang luar biasa jika pengendali terminal mengenakan caj terminal atau fi perkhidmatan penumpang. Namun, memberi mereka kawalan eksklusif terhadap penjualan tiket adalah perkara yang sama sekali berbeza.
Cadangan itu sukar dipertahankan dan bukanlah amalan biasa di tempat lain.
Terminal sepatutnya menyediakan kemudahan kepada perkhidmatan bas, bukannya mengawal jualan tiket mereka.
Industri bas ekspres Malaysia sejak sekian lama terikat dengan pendekatan perancangan pengangkutan awam yang terlalu berpusat kepada terminal.
Pengusaha diwajibkan menggunakan terminal tertentu tanpa mengambil kira sama ada lokasinya benar-benar mudah untuk penumpang atau mempunyai hubungan baik dengan sistem pengangkutan lain.
Pada masa sama, banyak terminal berkembang menjadi projek hartanah komersial yang melibatkan pelaburan besar dalam bangunan dan kemudahan, sekali gus perlu menjana pulangan.

Pengusaha bas perlu membayar caj terminal, manakala penumpang pula terpaksa menanggung kesulitan serta kos tambahan untuk pergi ke terminal yang mungkin tidak mempunyai perhubungan baik dengan destinasi sebenar mereka.
Keadaan menjadi lebih bermasalah apabila pengendali terminal turut diberikan kawalan eksklusif ke atas penjualan tiket.

Di bawah arahan baharu Apad, pengendali terminal akan mempunyai hak tunggal menjual tiket bagi perkhidmatan bas ekspres yang beroperasi dari terminal mereka. Mereka juga akan bertanggungjawab mengurus perjalanan, pelepasan bas dan transaksi penjualan tiket.
Ini menimbulkan satu lagi persoalan.

Jika pengusaha bas bertanggungjawab menjalankan perkhidmatan, menyelenggara kenderaan, menggaji pemandu dan mematuhi syarat keselamatan, mengapa mereka perlu menyerahkan kawalan terhadap jualan tiket sendiri?
Terminal menyediakan infrastruktur. Pengusaha bas pula menyediakan perkhidmatan pengangkutan.
Kedua-duanya menjalankan fungsi komersial yang berbeza. Tiada alasan kukuh untuk menggabungkannya melalui satu ketetapan wajib yang memberi satu pihak kawalan ke atas aliran pendapatan pihak lain.
Kementerian Pengangkutan wajar meneliti semula arahan Apad ini dengan serius sebelum ia berkuat kuasa.
